entries.literal: Escorts provisioned a boat as usual; Ge would none of it and took only the single craft the office provided.

entries.zh: 舸艚偏欹，不得安臥。
entries.en: The boat listed to one side, and he could not lie down in comfort.
entries.literal: The boat listed to one side—he could not lie at ease.

entries.zh: 或謂革曰：「船旣不平，濟江甚險，當移徙重物，以迮輕艚。」
entries.en: Someone told Ge, "The boat is unsteady. Crossing the river will be dangerous. Move heavy things to weigh down the lighter hull."
entries.literal: Someone said to Ge: "The boat is unsteady—crossing the river will be perilous; you should shift heavy objects to ballast the lighter hull."

entries.zh: 革旣無物，乃於西陵岸取石十餘片以實之。
entries.en: Ge owned nothing. He went to the West Mausoleum shore, took more than ten stones, and loaded them aboard.
entries.literal: Ge had nothing; he went to the West Mausoleum shore and took a dozen-odd stones to fill it.

entries.zh: 其清貧如此。
entries.en: Such was his austerity.
entries.literal: Such was his austerity and poverty.

entries.zh: 休源少孤，立志操，風範強正，明練治體。
entries.en: Orphaned young, Xiuyuan set his will and bearing early—resolute in character, clear in the ways of government.
entries.literal: Xiuyuan was orphaned young but established resolve and character—strong and upright in bearing, clear and practiced in governance.

entries.zh: 持身儉約，學窮文藝，當官理務，不憚強禦，常以天下爲己任。
entries.en: Frugal in private life, deeply learned in letters, fearless before the mighty in office, he always acted as though the empire rested on his shoulders.
entries.literal: He lived frugally, mastered literary arts, handled official duties without fearing the powerful, and always took the realm as his charge.

entries.zh: 高祖深委仗之。
entries.en: Gaozu relied on him completely.
entries.literal: The Emperor deeply entrusted him.

entries.zh: 累居顯職，纖毫無犯。
entries.en: Through one high appointment after another, he never committed the slightest fault.
entries.literal: Through successive high posts not the slightest offense was found.

entries.zh: 性慎密，寡嗜好。
entries.en: He was cautious by nature and had few appetites.
entries.literal: His nature was cautious and reserved, with few indulgences.

entries.zh: 出入帷幄，未嘗言禁中事，世以此重之。
entries.en: In and out of the inner councils he never breathed a word of palace affairs, and for that the world respected him.
entries.literal: Entering and leaving the inner councils he never spoke of palace secrets—and the world for this held him in esteem.

entries.zh: 聚書盈七千卷，手自校治，凡奏議彈文，勒成十五卷。
entries.en: He collected more than seven thousand books and collated them himself; his memorials and impeachments were gathered into fifteen fascicles.
entries.literal: He amassed more than seven thousand volumes of books and personally collated them; memorials and impeachments were compiled into fifteen fascicles.

entries.zh: 除尚書駕部郎。
entries.en: He was appointed Driving Section Director in the Masters of Writing.
entries.literal: Appointed Driving Section Director in the Masters of Writing.

entries.zh: 中興元年，高祖入石頭，時吳興太守袁昂據郡距義師，乃使革制書與昂，于坐立成，辭義典雅，高祖深賞歎之，因令與徐勉同掌書記。
entries.en: In the first year of Zhongxing Gaozu entered Stone Fort while Yuan Ang, administrator of Wuxing, held the commandery against the cause. Ge was told to draft the letter to Ang and finished it on the spot; its language was elegant, Gaozu praised it highly, and put him in charge of written records together with Xu Mian.
entries.literal: In the first year of Zhongxing the Emperor entered Stone Fort; at that time Yuan Ang, Administrator of Wuxing, held the commandery against the righteous army—Ge was sent to compose the imperial letter to Ang and finished it standing at the desk; its phrasing was elegant and classical, and the Emperor deeply admired it, then had him jointly manage written records with Xu Mian.

entries.zh: 建安王爲雍州刺史，表求管記，以革爲征北記室參軍，帶中廬令。
entries.en: When Prince of Jian'an became inspector of Yongzhou and asked for a chief secretary, Ge was made secretary to the northern expedition staff and concurrently magistrate of Zhonglu.
entries.literal: Prince of Jian'an was made Inspector of Yong province and requested a chief secretary; Ge was made Secretary to the Northern Expedition, concurrently Magistrate of Zhonglu.

entries.zh: 與弟觀少長共居，不忍離別，苦求同行，乃以觀爲征北行參軍，兼記室。
entries.en: He and Guan had lived together since childhood and could not bear to separate; Guan pleaded to go with him, and was made acting secretary on the northern expedition staff, additionally serving as secretary.
entries.literal: He and his brother Guan had lived together from youth and could not bear to part; Guan begged hard to go together, so Guan was made Acting Secretary to the Northern Expedition, additionally secretary.

entries.zh: 時吳興沈約、樂安任昉，並相賞重，昉與革書云：「此段雍府妙選英才，文房之職，總卿昆季，可謂馭二龍於長途，騁騏驥於千里。」
entries.en: Shen Yue of Wuxing and Ren Fang of Le'an both valued him. Fang wrote to Ge: "The Yongzhou staff has chosen its finest men—you and your brother both hold the literary office. It is like driving two dragons on a long road or running twin thoroughbreds a thousand li."
entries.literal: At the time Shen Yue of Wuxing and Ren Fang of Le'an both prized him; Fang wrote to Ge: "This segment of the Yong prefecture household is a fine selection of talent—the literary office, both you brothers hold it—one may say driving two dragons on a long road, galloping fine steeds a thousand li."

entries.zh: 途次江夏，觀遇疾卒。
entries.en: On the road at Jiangxia, Guan fell ill and died.
entries.literal: En route at Jiangxia, Guan fell ill and died.

entries.zh: 革時在雍，爲府王所禮，款若布衣。
entries.en: Ge was then in Yongzhou, and the prince treated him with the easy warmth of an old friend.
entries.literal: Ge was then in Yong, treated by the prince with the warmth of a commoner's friendship.

entries.zh: 王被徵爲丹陽尹，以革爲記室，領五官掾，除通直散騎常侍，建康正。
entries.en: When the prince was recalled as magistrate of Danyang, Ge became his secretary, head of the Five Officials section, Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, and chief of Jiankang.
entries.literal: The prince was summoned as Magistrate of Danyang; Ge was made secretary, overseeing the Five Officials Aide, appointed Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, and Chief of Jiankang.

entries.zh: 頻遷秣陵、建康令。
entries.en: He was promoted in turn to magistrate of Moling and Jiankang.
entries.literal: Repeatedly promoted to Magistrate of Moling and Jiankang.

entries.zh: 爲治明肅，豪強憚之。
entries.en: He governed with clarity and severity, and the local strongmen feared him.
entries.literal: His governance was clear and stern—the powerful feared him.

entries.zh: 入爲中書舍人，尚書左丞，司農卿，復出爲雲麾晉安王長史、尋陽太守、行江州府事。
entries.en: He entered court as Palace Writer Attendant, Left Assistant Director of the Masters of Writing, and Minister of Agriculture, then went out again as chief clerk to Prince Jin'an of Cloud Banner, administrator of Xunyang, and acting head of Jiangzhou affairs.
entries.literal: He entered as Palace Writer Attendant, Left Assistant Director of the Ministry of Works, and Minister of Agriculture; then went out again as Chief Clerk to Prince Jin'an of Cloud Banner, Administrator of Xunyang, and overseer of Jiangzhou prefectural affairs.

entries.zh: 徙仁威廬陵王長史，太守、行事如故，以清嚴爲百城所憚。
entries.en: Transferred to chief clerk for Prince Renwei of Luling, he kept the same administrator and acting duties, and commanderies across the realm feared his austerity.
entries.literal: He was transferred as Chief Clerk to Prince Renwei of Luling; his posts as administrator and acting deputy remained unchanged, and every commandery feared him for his probity and severity.

entries.zh: 時少王行事多傾意于簽帥，革以正直自居，不與簽帥等同坐。
entries.en: Young princes' acting deputies usually bowed to their chiefs of staff; Ge stood on principle and refused to share a seat with them.
entries.literal: At the time young princes' acting deputies often deferred to their chiefs of staff; Ge held himself to rectitude and would not sit with chiefs of staff as equals.

entries.zh: 俄遷左光祿大夫、南平王長史、御史中丞，彈奏豪權，一無所避。
entries.en: Soon he rose to Left Grand Master of Lustrous Virtue, chief clerk to Prince Nanping, and censor-in-chief, impeaching the mighty without flinching.
entries.literal: Soon he was promoted to Left Grand Master of Lustrous Virtue, Chief Clerk to Prince Nanping, and Censor-in-Chief, impeaching powerful magnates without evasion.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：高祖留心政道，孔休源以識治見知，旣遇其時，斯爲幸矣。
entries.en: The historian writes: Gaozu cared for good government. Kong Xiuyuan was known for his grasp of rule, and to meet such a time was fortune.
entries.literal: The historian writes: Gaozu attended to governance; Kong Xiuyuan was recognized for his discernment in administration—having met his time, this was fortune.

entries.zh: 江革聰敏亮直，亦一代之盛名歟。
entries.en: Jiang Ge was quick, bright, and upright—a famed name of his generation, surely.
entries.literal: Jiang Ge was quick-witted, brilliant, and upright—is he not a famed name of his generation?

entries.zh: 次子從簡，少有文情，年十七，作《采荷詞》以刺敬容，爲當時所賞。
entries.en: Second son Congjian had literary feeling from youth. At seventeen he wrote "Song of Gathering Lotus" to satirize Jingrong, and his age praised it.
entries.literal: Second son Congjian had literary sensibility from youth; at seventeen he wrote "Song of Gathering Lotus" to satirize Jingrong and won acclaim in his day.

entries.zh: 歷官司徒從事中郎。
entries.en: He served as aide to the Minister of Education.
entries.literal: He served as aide to the Minister of Education.

entries.zh: 侯景亂，爲任約所害。
entries.en: In Hou Jing's rebellion Ren Yue killed him.
entries.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he was killed by Ren Yue.

entries.zh: 子兼叩頭流血，乞代父命，以身蔽刃，遂俱見殺。
entries.en: His son Jian kowtowed until blood ran, begging to die in his father's place and covering him with his body. Both were killed.
entries.literal: His son Jian kowtowed until blood flowed, begging to die in his father's place and shielding him with his body—they were both killed.

entries.zh: 天下莫不痛之。
entries.en: All under heaven grieved.
entries.literal: All under heaven grieved.

entries.zh: 梁書卷第三十六 列傳第三十
entries.en: Book of Liang, Volume 36, Biography 30
entries.literal: Book of Liang, Volume 36, Biography 30

entries.zh: 起家秘書郎，遷太子舍人，輕車功曹史，秘書丞，司空從事中郎，太子庶子，家令，掌東宮管記，深爲昭明太子賞接。
entries.en: He entered service as a Secretariat gentleman, then rose through posts as heir-apparent attendant, merit-office secretary, secretariat aide, masters-of-works attendant, crown-prince household administrator, and household master, overseeing the Eastern Palace archives, and won the deep favor of Crown Prince Zhaoming.
entries.literal: He began his career as Secretary Gentleman, was transferred to Attendant of the Heir Apparent, Secretary Gentleman of the Light Chariot Merit Office, Secretariat Assistant, Attendant Gentleman of the Masters of Works, Crown Prince’s Household Administrator, and Household Master; he managed the Eastern Palace record office and was deeply favored by Crown Prince Zhaoming.

entries.zh: 秘書監任昉出爲新安郡，別舉詩云：「詎念耋嗟人，方深老夫託。」
entries.en: When Ren Fang, Director of the Secretariat, left for Xin’an Commandery, he sent Ju a farewell poem: “I would not dwell on the groaning elder—yet how deeply I place my trust in you, old friend.”
entries.literal: When Secretariat Director Ren Fang went out to Xin’an Commandery, he parted with a poem to Ju saying: “How could I think of the sighing old man—yet how deeply I entrust myself to you, my elder friend.”

entries.zh: 其屬意如此。
entries.en: Such was the feeling he meant to convey.
entries.literal: His intent was of this sort.

entries.zh: 嘗侍宴華林園，高祖訪舉於覽，覽對曰：「識藝過臣甚遠，惟飲酒不及於臣。」
entries.en: Once at a banquet in Huaglin Garden the Founding Emperor asked Lan about Ju; Lan answered: “His learning and skill far exceed mine—only in wine he cannot match me.”
entries.literal: Once while attending a banquet in Huaglin Garden, the Founding Emperor inquired about Ju through Lan; Lan replied: “His knowledge and talent far surpass mine; only in drinking he does not equal me.”

entries.zh: 高祖大悅。
entries.en: The Founding Emperor was delighted.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor was greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 轉太子中庶子，猶掌管記。
entries.en: He was made an attendant in the heir’s palace while continuing to keep the archives.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Attendant of the Crown Prince’s Palace, still managing the records.

entries.zh: 敬容身長八尺，白皙美鬚眉。
entries.en: Jingrong stood eight chi tall, with fair skin and handsome beard and brows.
entries.literal: Jingrong’s stature was eight chi; he was fair-skinned with handsome beard and brows.

entries.zh: 性矜莊，衣冠尤事鮮麗，每公庭就列，容止出人。
entries.en: Proud and formal by nature, he lavished care on bright, elegant dress; whenever he took his place at court his bearing outshone the rest.
entries.literal: His nature was proud and dignified; above all he paid attention to fresh and beautiful dress, and whenever he took his place in public assembly his bearing exceeded other men.

entries.zh: 三年，遷尚書右僕射，參掌選事，侍中如故。
entries.en: In the third year he became Right Vice Director of the Secretariat and shared in appointments, still Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: In the third year he was transferred to Right Vice Director of the Secretariat and participated in selection affairs, his status as Palace Attendant remaining.

entries.zh: 時僕射徐勉參掌機密，以疾陳解，因舉敬容自代，故有此授焉。
entries.en: Vice Director Xu Mian then held the secret reins of power; when he resigned on grounds of illness he recommended Jingrong to succeed him, and so the post fell to him.
entries.literal: At the time Vice Director Xu Mian managed secret affairs; citing illness he resigned, and therefore nominated Jingrong to replace him—hence this appointment.

entries.zh: 五年，遷左僕射，加宣惠將軍，置佐史，侍中、參掌如故。
entries.en: In the fifth year he was made Left Vice Director and General Who Spreads Grace, with clerks assigned, while he remained Palace Attendant and kept his role in administration.
entries.literal: In the fifth year he was transferred to Left Vice Director, with the added title of General Who Spreads Grace, staff clerks appointed, his status as Palace Attendant and participation in management remaining.

entries.zh: 大同三年正月，朱雀門災，高祖謂羣臣曰：「此門制卑狹，我始欲構，遂遭天火。」
entries.en: In the first month of the third year of Datong the Vermilion Bird Gate burned; the Founding Emperor told the ministers: “The gate was built too low and cramped—I had only just meant to rebuild it when Heaven sent this blaze.”
entries.literal: In the first month of the third year of Datong, the Vermilion Bird Gate caught fire; the Founding Emperor said to the assembled ministers: “This gate was made low and narrow; I had just intended to rebuild it when Heaven sent this fire.”

entries.zh: 並相顧未有答。
entries.en: The courtiers looked at one another and none answered.
entries.literal: They all looked at one another without any reply.

entries.zh: 敬容獨曰：「此所謂陛下『先天而天不違』。」
entries.en: Only Jingrong spoke: “This is what Your Majesty calls acting before Heaven so that Heaven does not oppose you.”
entries.literal: Jingrong alone said: “This is what Your Majesty means when you ‘act before Heaven, and Heaven does not contradict you.’”

entries.zh: 時以爲名對。
entries.en: Men at the time hailed it as a brilliant reply.
entries.literal: The time regarded this as a celebrated retort.

entries.zh: 俄遷中權將軍、丹陽尹，侍中、參掌、佐史如故。
entries.en: Soon he was made Central Authority General and Intendant of Danyang, keeping Palace Attendant, his administrative role, and his staff.
entries.literal: Shortly he was transferred to Central Authority General and Intendant of Danyang, his status as Palace Attendant, participation in affairs, and staff clerks remaining.

entries.zh: 五年，入爲尚書令，侍中、將軍、參掌、佐史如故。
entries.en: In the fifth year he returned as Director of the Secretariat, still Palace Attendant, general, administrator, and chief clerk.
entries.literal: In the fifth year he entered court as Director of the Secretariat, his status as Palace Attendant, General, participation in affairs, and staff clerks remaining.

entries.zh: 中大同元年三月，高祖幸同泰寺講《金字三慧經》，敬容請預聽，敕許之。
entries.en: In the third month of the first year of Zhongdatong the Founding Emperor went to Tongtai Temple to expound the Golden-character Three Wisdom Sutra; Jingrong asked to hear it and was allowed by edict.
entries.literal: In the third month of the first year of Zhongdatong, the Founding Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to lecture on the Golden-character Three Wisdom Sutra; Jingrong asked to attend and was permitted by edict.

entries.zh: 又有敕聽朔望問訊。
entries.en: Another edict let him attend the new- and full-moon audiences to offer greetings.
entries.literal: There was also an edict allowing him to pay court on the new and full moon for ritual inquiries.

entries.zh: 尋起爲金紫光祿大夫，未拜，又加侍中。
entries.en: Soon he was recalled as Grand Master with the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon; before he could accept it he was again made Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: Before long he was restored as Grand Master with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon; before he accepted the seal he was again promoted to Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 敬容舊時賓客門生喧嘩如昔，冀其復用。
entries.en: His old clients and students raised the same clamor as before, hoping he would be used again.
entries.literal: Jingrong’s former clients and disciples made as loud a commotion as of old, hoping he would be reemployed.

entries.zh: 會稽謝鬱致書戒之曰：「草萊之人，聞諸道路，君侯已得瞻望朝夕，出入禁門，醉尉將不敢呵，灰然不無其漸，甚休，甚休！
entries.en: Xie Yu of Kuaiji wrote to warn him: “From common report we hear that you may once more gaze on the court at dawn and dusk and pass the palace gates—that even the drunken gate guard will not bark at you—yet the slope is not absent; how fortunate, how fortunate!
entries.literal: Xie Yu of Kuaiji sent him a letter of admonition saying: “A man of the fields, hearing talk on the road, learns that you may again look upon the court morning and evening, pass in and out of the forbidden gates, and that the drunken gatekeeper will not dare to shout you down—yet there is no lack of a gradual slide; most fortunate, most fortunate!

entries.zh: 敢賀於前，又將吊也。
entries.en: I congratulate you beforehand—and I must mourn you as well.
entries.literal: I venture congratulations in advance, yet I must also offer condolences.

entries.zh: 昔流言裁作，公旦東奔；
entries.en: When rumor first arose, the Duke of Zhou fled east;
entries.literal: In olden days when slander spread, the Duke of Zhou fled east;

entries.zh: 燕書始來，子孟不入。
entries.en: when the letter from Yan came, Zi Meng would not go in.
entries.literal: when the Yan letter first arrived, Zi Meng would not enter.

entries.zh: 夫聖賢被虛過以自斥，未有嬰時釁而求親者也。
entries.en: Sages have been slandered and therefore held themselves back; no wise man has ever sought intimacy at a time of blame.
entries.literal: Sages and worthies have been reproached on false charges and therefore restrained themselves; never has one courted favor at a moment of scandal.

entries.zh: 且曝鰓之鱗，不念杯杓之水；
entries.en: Fish with drying gills do not think of a cup of water;
entries.literal: Moreover, fish with gills laid bare do not think of a cup of water;

entries.zh: 雲霄之翼，豈顧籠樊之糧。
entries.en: wings that touch the clouds do not glance at fodder in a pen.
entries.literal: wings that reach the clouds do not look back at grain in a cage.

entries.zh: 何者？
entries.en: Why?
entries.literal: Why?

entries.zh: 所托已盛也。
entries.en: Because what they rest on is already vast.
entries.literal: What they rely on is already great.

entries.zh: 昔君侯納言加首，鳴玉在腰，回豊貂以步文昌，聳高蟬而趨武帳，可謂盛矣。
entries.en: Once, when you were chief minister, jade chimed at your belt; you swept sable robes as you entered Wenchang and lifted your cicada crest as you hastened to the martial hall—truly a time of glory.
entries.literal: In former days when you were chief counsellor, jade tinkled at your waist; you turned rich sable as you walked to Wenchang and raised high your cicada hat as you hurried to the military hall—one might call that splendor indeed.

entries.zh: 不以此時薦才拔士，少報聖主之恩；
entries.en: You did not then lift men of talent to repay your sovereign’s kindness;
entries.literal: You did not then recommend talent and advance scholars to repay the sage ruler’s grace;

entries.zh: 今卒如爰絲之說，受責見過，方復欲更窺朝廷，觖望萬分，竊不爲左右取也。
entries.en: now, as Master Ai’s words have it, you bear blame and fault, yet you would look again toward the court and hope for the slightest chance—I cannot think this wise for you.
entries.literal: now at last, as Master Ai’s saying goes, you are blamed and found at fault, yet you would again peer into court and hope for a ten-thousandth chance—I do not think this wise for you.

entries.zh: 昔竇嬰、楊惲亦得罪明時，不能謝絕賓客，猶交黨援，卒無後福，終益前禍。
entries.en: Dou Ying and Yang Yun too offended a luminous court; unable to shut their doors to guests, they still traded on connections, and in the end won no blessing but deepened their fall.
entries.literal: In olden days Dou Ying and Yang Yun also fell from favor in a bright age; they could not cut off their clients and still kept up factional ties, and in the end found no lasting blessing but only added to their former disaster.

entries.zh: 僕之所吊，實在於斯。
entries.en: My condolences are for this very thing.
entries.literal: What I mourn is precisely this.

entries.zh: 人人所以頗猶有踵君侯之門者，未必皆感惠懷仁，有灌夫、任安之義，乃戒翟公之大署，冀君侯之復用也。
entries.en: Those who still throng your door are not all moved by grace or bound like Guan Fu and Ren An; they dread Duke Zhai’s famous notice and hope for your return to power.
entries.literal: The reason men still somewhat crowd your gate is not necessarily that they feel your kindness or owe you the loyalty of Guan Fu or Ren An; they fear Duke Zhai’s great inscription and hope you will be used again.

entries.zh: 夫在思過之日，而挾復用之意，未可爲智者說矣。
entries.en: To cling to hope of office while you should be repenting is not counsel fit for a wise man.
entries.literal: To harbor hope of reuse on a day meant for reflection on faults is not something one can explain to the wise.

entries.zh: 君侯宜杜門念失，無有所通，築茅茨于鐘阜，聊優遊以卒歲，見可憐之意，著待終之情。
entries.en: Shut your door, ponder your fault, deal with no one, raise a thatched hut on Bell Peak, and live out your days at leisure, showing that you accept reproach and await your end.
entries.literal: You ought to shut your door and dwell on your error, have no dealings with others, build a thatched hut on Bell Mountain, and pass your remaining years in ease, showing a mind open to pity and a spirit ready for the end.

entries.zh: 復仲尼能改之言，惟子貢更也之譬，少戢言於衆口，微自救於竹帛，所謂『失之東隅，收之桑榆』。
entries.en: Remember that Confucius said a man may mend his ways, and Zigong that one may change; speak less to the multitude and rescue yourself a little on the page—that is “what is lost at sunrise is gained at sunset.”
entries.literal: Take again Confucius’s words that one can reform, and Zigong’s saying that one may change; curb your speech in the crowd and save yourself a little in the record—this is what is called losing in the east corner and gaining in the mulberry west.

entries.zh: 如此，令明主聞知，尚有冀也。
entries.en: Do this, and if the wise sovereign learns of it, hope may yet remain.
entries.literal: If you do so, the enlightened ruler may hear of it and there will still be hope.

entries.zh: 僕東皋鄙人，入穴幸無銜窶，恥天下之士不爲執事道之，故披肝膽，示情素，君侯豈能鑒焉。」
entries.en: I am a humble man of the eastern shore; though I live apart I am not ashamed to speak; I blush that no gentleman in the realm speaks frankly to you, and so I bare my inmost heart—will you not see it?”
entries.literal: I am a rustic of the eastern marshes; though I have gone into hiding I am not yet ashamed to speak; I blush that gentlemen under heaven do not speak for you as they should, and so I lay bare my liver and show my heart—can you not discern it?”

entries.zh: 十一年，坐妾弟費慧明爲導倉丞，夜盜官米，爲禁司所執，送領軍府。
entries.en: In the eleventh year his concubine’s younger brother Fei Huiming, a grain-depot clerk, stole government grain by night; the patrol seized him and handed him to the Rear Guard command.
entries.literal: In the eleventh year his concubine’s younger brother Fei Huiming served as grain depot clerk; at night he stole official grain, was seized by the prohibition officers, and sent to the Army of the Rear Guard headquarters.

entries.zh: 時河東王譽爲領軍將軍，敬容以書解慧明，譽即封書以奏。
entries.en: Prince of Hedong Xiao Yu then commanded the Rear Guard; Jingrong wrote to plead for Huiming, and Yu at once sealed the letter and reported it to the throne.
entries.literal: At the time Prince of Hedong Yu was General of the Rear Guard; Jingrong wrote a letter interceding for Huiming, and Yu immediately sealed the letter and memorialized it.

entries.zh: 高祖大怒，付南司推劾。
entries.en: The Founding Emperor was enraged and sent the case to the Southern Office for prosecution.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor was furious and handed him over to the Southern Office for investigation.

entries.zh: 御史中丞張綰奏敬容挾私罔上，合棄市刑，詔特免職。
entries.en: Censor Zhang Wan charged that Jingrong had used private ties to mislead the throne and deserved death; an edict spared his life but stripped him of office.
entries.literal: Censor-in-Chief Zhang Zan memorialized that Jingrong practiced favoritism and deceived his sovereign, deserving execution; the edict specially exempted him only from office.

entries.zh: 初，天監中，有沙門釋寶志者，嘗遇敬容，謂曰：「君後必貴，然終是何敗何耳」。
entries.en: Earlier, in the Tianjian era, the monk Baozhi had met him and said: “You are sure to reach the heights, yet in the end—what defeat, what?”
entries.literal: Earlier in the Tianjian era the monk Baozhi had once met Jingrong and said: “You will certainly rise to eminence, yet in the end—what defeat, what?”

entries.zh: 及敬容爲宰相，謂何姓當爲其禍，故抑沒宗族，無仕進者，至是竟爲河東所敗。
entries.en: Once he was chancellor he feared harm from anyone surnamed He and blocked his clan from office; in the end he was brought down by the Prince of Hedong.
entries.literal: When Jingrong became chancellor he thought the He surname would be his calamity, so he suppressed his clan and none obtained advancement; in the end he was indeed ruined by Hedong.

entries.zh: 太清二年，遷尚書令，侍中、將軍如故。
entries.en: In the second year of Taiqing he became Director of the Secretariat, still Palace Attendant and general.
entries.literal: In the second year of Taiqing he was transferred to Director of the Secretariat, remaining Palace Attendant and General.

entries.zh: 是歲，侯景寇京師，舉卒于圍內。
entries.en: That year, when Hou Jing besieged the capital, Ju died inside the encircled city.
entries.literal: That year, when Hou Jing attacked the capital, Ju died within the siege.

entries.zh: 詔贈侍中、中衛將軍、開府儀同三司，侍中、尚書令如故。
entries.en: An edict mourned him with Palace Attendant, Central Guard General, and Grand Honorific with the Three Insignia, while his posts as Palace Attendant and Director of the Secretariat stood unchanged.
entries.literal: The edict posthumously awarded him Palace Attendant, Central Guard General, and Grand Honorific with the Three Insignia, his offices of Palace Attendant and Director of the Secretariat remaining.

entries.zh: 文集亂中並亡逸。
entries.en: His collected works perished entirely in the upheaval.
entries.literal: His collected writings were all lost in the disorders.

entries.zh: 太清元年，遷太子詹事，侍中如故。
entries.en: In Taiqing 1, he was transferred to Crown Prince's Household Administrator, remaining Attendant-in-Ordinary as before.
entries.literal: In Taiqing 1, he was transferred to Crown Prince's Household Administrator, remaining Attendant-in-Ordinary as before.

entries.zh: 二年，侯景襲京師，敬容自府移家臺內。
entries.en: In the second year, when Hou Jing attacked the capital, Jingrong moved his household from his office into the imperial compound.
entries.literal: In the second year, when Hou Jing attacked the capital, Jingrong moved his household from his office into the imperial compound.

entries.zh: 初，景于渦陽退敗，未得審實，傳者乃云其將暴顯反，景身與衆並沒，朝廷以爲憂。
entries.en: Earlier, when Jing had been defeated at Guoyang and no verified report had yet arrived, rumor said that his general Bao Xian had rebelled and that Jing himself and his troops had all perished, and the court was anxious over it.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Jing had been defeated at Guoyang and no verified report had yet arrived, rumor said that his general Bao Xian had rebelled and that Jing himself and his troops had all perished, and the court was anxious over it.

entries.zh: 敬容尋見東宮，太宗謂曰：「淮北始更有信，侯景定得身免，不如所傳。」
entries.en: Jingrong soon had an audience in the Eastern Palace, and Taizong said to him, "News has only just come again from north of the Huai: Hou Jing certainly escaped alive, not as the rumors said."
entries.literal: Jingrong soon had an audience in the Eastern Palace, and Taizong said to him, "News has only just come again from north of the Huai: Hou Jing certainly escaped alive, not as the rumors said."

entries.zh: 敬容對曰：「得景遂死，深是朝廷之福。」
entries.en: Jingrong replied, "If Jing had indeed died, it would be a great blessing for the court."
entries.literal: Jingrong replied, "If Jing had indeed died, it would be a great blessing for the court."

entries.zh: 太宗失色，問其故。
entries.en: Taizong turned pale and asked the reason.
entries.literal: Taizong turned pale and asked the reason.

entries.zh: 敬容曰：「景翻覆叛臣，終當亂國。」
entries.en: Jingrong said, "Jing is a treacherous rebel minister; in the end he will throw the state into disorder."
entries.literal: Jingrong said, "Jing is a treacherous rebel minister; in the end he will throw the state into disorder."

entries.zh: 是年，太宗頻於玄圃自講《老》《莊》二書，學士吳孜時寄詹事府，每日入聽。
entries.en: That year Taizong often personally lectured on the Laozi and Zhuangzi at Xuanpu. The scholar Wu Zi was then attached to the Crown Prince's Household Administrator's office and entered every day to listen.
entries.literal: That year Taizong often personally lectured on the Laozi and Zhuangzi at Xuanpu. The scholar Wu Zi was then attached to the Crown Prince's Household Administrator's office and entered every day to listen.

entries.zh: 敬容謂孜曰：「昔晉代喪亂，頗由祖尚玄虛，胡賊殄覆中夏。
entries.en: Jingrong said to Zi, "In the past, the disasters and disorder of the Jin were largely due to esteeming abstruse emptiness, and Hu bandits destroyed the central realm.
entries.literal: Jingrong said to Zi, "In the past, the disasters and disorder of the Jin were largely due to esteeming abstruse emptiness, and Hu bandits destroyed the central realm.

entries.zh: 今東宮復襲此，殆非人事，其將爲戎乎？」
entries.en: Now the Eastern Palace is taking this up again. This scarcely seems like a human matter; is it about to become a barbarian calamity?"
entries.literal: Now the Eastern Palace is taking this up again. This scarcely seems like a human matter; is it about to become a barbarian calamity?"

entries.zh: 俄而侯景難作，其言有徵也。
entries.en: Soon Hou Jing's calamity broke out, and his words were borne out.
entries.literal: Soon Hou Jing's calamity broke out, and his words were borne out.

entries.zh: 三年正月，敬容卒于圍內，詔贈仁威將軍，本官並如故。
entries.en: In the first month of the third year, Jingrong died inside the siege. An edict posthumously granted him the title General of Benevolent Awe, with all his regular offices as before.
entries.literal: In the first month of the third year, Jingrong died inside the siege. An edict posthumously granted him the title General of Benevolent Awe, with all his regular offices as before.

entries.zh: 敬容以名家子，弱冠選尚齊武帝女長城公主，拜駙馬都尉。
entries.en: Jingrong, as the son of a distinguished house, was selected in his early twenties to marry Emperor Wu of Qi's daughter, Princess Changcheng, and was appointed Commandant of the Horse Guards.
entries.literal: Jingrong, as the son of a distinguished house, was selected in his early twenties to marry Emperor Wu of Qi's daughter, Princess Changcheng, and was appointed Commandant of the Horse Guards.

entries.zh: 天監初，爲秘書郎，歷太子舍人，尚書殿中郎，太子洗馬，中書舍人，秘書丞，遷揚州治中。
entries.en: At the beginning of Tianjian he became Palace Library Gentleman, and then served successively as crown prince attendant, Palace Gentleman in the Department of State Affairs, Groom of the Crown Prince, Secretariat Drafter, and Assistant Director of the Palace Library, before being transferred to administrative aide of Yangzhou.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Tianjian he became Palace Library Gentleman, and then served successively as crown prince attendant, Palace Gentleman in the Department of State Affairs, Groom of the Crown Prince, Secretariat Drafter, and Assistant Director of the Palace Library, before being transferred to administrative aide of Yangzhou.

entries.zh: 出爲建安內史，清公有美績，民吏稱之。
entries.en: He went out as Interior Minister of Jian'an, where he was honest and fair and achieved an excellent record, and the people and officials praised him.
entries.literal: He went out as Interior Minister of Jian'an, where he was honest and fair and achieved an excellent record, and the people and officials praised him.

entries.zh: 還除黃門郎，累遷太子中庶子，散騎常侍，侍中，司徒左長史。
entries.en: On returning to court he was appointed Yellow Gate Gentleman, then rose successively to Junior Mentor in the heir apparent's household, Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, Attendant-in-Ordinary, and left chief clerk to the Minister over the Masses.
entries.literal: On returning to court he was appointed Yellow Gate Gentleman, then rose successively to Household Attendant to the Crown Prince, Regular Attendant, Attendant-in-Ordinary, and left chief clerk to the Minister over the Masses.

entries.zh: 普通二年，復爲侍中，領羽林監，俄又領本州大中正。
entries.en: In the second year of Putong, he again became Attendant-in-Ordinary, concurrently Director of the Feathered Forest Guard, and soon also served as Grand Rectifier of his home province.
entries.literal: In Putong 2, he again became Attendant-in-Ordinary, concurrently director of the Feathered Forest Guard, and soon also served as grand rectifier of his home province.

entries.zh: 頃之，守吏部尚書，銓序明審，號爲稱職。
entries.en: Before long, he acted as Minister of Personnel; his selection and ordering of officials were clear and careful, and he was considered competent in the post.
entries.literal: Before long, he acted as Minister of Personnel; his selection and ordering of officials were clear and careful, and he was considered competent in the post.

entries.zh: 四年，出爲招遠將軍、吳郡太守，爲政勤恤民隱，辨訟如神，視事四年，治爲天下第一。
entries.en: In the fourth year, he went out as General Who Summons the Distant and administrator of Wu Commandery. In governing he diligently cared for the people's hardships and judged lawsuits with almost uncanny precision. After four years in office, his administration was ranked first in the realm.
entries.literal: In the fourth year, he went out as General Who Summons the Distant and administrator of Wu Commandery. In governing he diligently cared for the people's hardships and judged lawsuits with almost uncanny precision. After four years in office, his administration was ranked first in the realm.

entries.zh: 吏民詣闕請樹碑，詔許之。
entries.en: The officials and people went to the palace gate to request permission to erect a stele, and an edict allowed it.
entries.literal: The officials and people went to the palace gate to request permission to erect a stele, and an edict allowed it.

entries.zh: 大通二年，徵爲中書令，未拜，復爲吏部尚書，領右軍將軍，俄加侍中。
entries.en: In Datong 2, he was summoned as Secretariat Director, but before taking office he was again made Minister of Personnel, concurrently General of the Right Army, and soon additionally Attendant-in-Ordinary.
entries.literal: In Datong 2, he was summoned as Secretariat Director, but before taking office he was again made Minister of Personnel, concurrently General of the Right Army, and soon additionally Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 中大通元年，改太子中庶子。
entries.en: In Zhongdatong 1, he was changed to Household Attendant to the Crown Prince.
entries.literal: In Zhongdatong 1, he was changed to Household Attendant to the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 梁書卷第三十七 列傳第三十一
entries.en: Book of Liang, Volume 37, Biography 31
entries.literal: Book of Liang, Volume 37, Biography 31

entries.zh: 舊制，年二十五方得釋褐。
entries.en: By longstanding custom, men did not enter office until twenty-five.
entries.literal: Under the old rule, one had to be twenty-five before shedding coarse dress for office.

entries.zh: 時异適二十一，特敕擢爲揚州議曹從事史。
entries.en: Yi was just twenty-one, yet an exceptional order promoted him to clerk in Yang Province’s council office.
entries.literal: Yi was then only twenty-one, but a special edict raised him to Clerk in the Council Office of Yang Province.

entries.zh: 尋有詔求異能之士，《五經》博士明山賓表薦异曰：「竊見錢唐朱异，年時尚少，德備老成。
entries.en: Before long the court called for exceptional talent; Five Classics Erudite Ming Shanbin recommended Yi, writing, "I have seen Zhu Yi of Qiantang—young in years, yet already mature in conduct.
entries.literal: Soon an edict sought men of outstanding ability; the Erudite of the Five Classics Ming Shanbin memorialized recommending Yi, saying: "I have observed Qiantang’s Zhu Yi—still young in years, yet complete in the virtue of age.

entries.zh: 在獨無散逸之想，處暗有對賓之色，器宇弘深，神表峰峻。
entries.en: In solitude he shows no wandering mind; in quiet he keeps the composure of a host receiving guests—his bearing is vast, his presence steep and bright.
entries.literal: Alone he harbors no thoughts of dissipation; in seclusion he bears the bearing of one facing guests; his capacity is broad and deep, his spirit lofty and sharp.

entries.zh: 金山萬丈，緣陟未登；
entries.en: A golden mountain rises ten thousand feet, yet its summit is still unscaled;
entries.literal: A golden mountain ten thousand feet high—one has not yet climbed its heights;

entries.zh: 玉海千尋，窺映不測。
entries.en: a jade ocean stretches a thousand fathoms, and no eye can plumb it.
entries.literal: a jade sea a thousand fathoms deep—gaze into it and its depths cannot be measured.

entries.zh: 加以珪璋新琢，錦組初構，觸響鏗鏘，值采便發。
entries.en: His jade is newly polished, his brocade freshly woven—strike him and the tone rings true; set him a task and he answers on the spot.
entries.literal: Add to this that his jade tablet is freshly cut and his brocade cords newly tied—strike it and the ring is clear; touch its colors and it answers at once.

entries.zh: 觀其信行，非惟十室所稀，若使負重遙途，必有千里之用。」
entries.en: Judge his trustworthiness and action: he is scarce even among ten households; set him to carry weight over a long road and he will go a thousand li."
entries.literal: Consider his faith and conduct: they are rare not merely in one household; if you set him to bear a heavy burden on a long road, he will surely serve for a thousand li."

entries.zh: 高祖召見，使說《孝經》、《周易》義，甚悅之，謂左右曰：「朱异實異。」
entries.en: The Founding Emperor received him, heard him lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety and the Book of Changes, and delighted in him, telling his attendants, "Zhu Yi is indeed exceptional."
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor summoned him, had him expound the Classic of Filial Piety and the Book of Changes, was greatly pleased, and said to those beside him: "Zhu Yi is truly extraordinary."

entries.zh: 後見明山賓，謂曰：「卿所舉殊得其人。」
entries.en: Later, meeting Ming Shanbin, he said, "Your recommendation hit the mark."
entries.literal: Later, seeing Ming Shanbin, he said: "The man you recommended is truly the right one."

entries.zh: 仍召异直西省，俄兼太學博士。
entries.en: He called Yi to regular duty in the Western Secretariat and shortly made him an erudite of the Imperial Academy as well.
entries.literal: He then summoned Yi to the Western Secretariat on permanent duty and soon added the post of Erudite of the Imperial Academy.

entries.zh: 其年，高祖自講《孝經》，使异執讀。
entries.en: In that year the emperor personally expounded the Classic of Filial Piety and appointed Yi to hold the book and read.
entries.literal: That year the Founding Emperor himself lectured on the Classic of Filial Piety and had Yi hold the text and read aloud.

entries.zh: 遷尚書儀曹郎，入兼中書通事舍人，累遷鴻臚卿，太子右衛率，尋加員外常侍。
entries.en: He rose to gentleman in the secretariat’s ceremonial office, served concurrently as a palace secretariat attendant, and climbed through chamberlain for dependencies, right commandant of the heir’s guards, and supernumerary palace attendant.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Gentleman of the Ceremonial Office of the Secretariat, entered service concurrently as Palace Secretariat Attendant, and was promoted in succession to Chamberlain for Dependencies, Right Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guards, and then Supernumerary Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 遷員外散騎常侍。
entries.en: He was promoted to supernumerary attendant of the discretionary cavalry.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Supernumerary Regular Attendant of the Discretionary Cavalry.

entries.zh: 舊尚書南坐，無貂；
entries.en: By old custom ministers of the southern secretariat wore no sable;
entries.literal: Formerly, when the Ministers sat facing south, they wore no sable;

entries.zh: 貂自琛始也。
entries.en: Chen was the first to wear it.
entries.literal: the sable began with Chen.

entries.zh: 頃之，遷御史中丞，參禮儀事如先。
entries.en: Soon he became censor-in-chief and continued to share in ritual matters as before.
entries.literal: Before long he was promoted to Censor-in-Chief, participating in ritual affairs as before.

entries.zh: 琛家產旣豊，買主第爲宅，爲有司所奏，坐免官。
entries.en: Chen's family was already wealthy; he purchased a former imperial mansion and was impeached and dismissed.
entries.literal: Chen's household wealth was already great; he bought an imperial residence for his mansion and was impeached by the responsible officials, losing his post for it.

entries.zh: 俄復爲尚書左丞，遷給事黃門侍郎，兼國子博士，未拜，改爲通直散騎常侍，領尚書左丞，並參禮儀事。
entries.en: He was soon restored as left assistant director of the Secretariat, then attendant gentleman of the yellow gates and concurrent erudite of the National University—before taking the latter he was made regular-attendance adviser of the discretionary cavalry, still left assistant director and still in charge of ritual.
entries.literal: Soon he was again made Left Assistant Director of the Secretariat, promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates, concurrently Erudite of the National University—before taking that post he was changed to Regular-attendance Adviser of the Discretionary Cavalry, holding the post of Left Assistant Director and sharing in ritual affairs as before.

entries.zh: 琛前後居職，凡郊廟諸儀，多所創定。
entries.en: In every post he helped shape suburban rites and much of the court's ceremonial code.
entries.literal: Throughout his successive offices, in suburban rites and all ritual matters he initiated and fixed many provisions.

entries.zh: 每見高祖，與語常移晷刻，故省中爲之語曰：「上殿不下有賀雅。」
entries.en: Audiences with Emperor Gaozu often ran long, and secretariat wits joked, "He who goes up to court and never comes down—that's Elegant He."
entries.literal: Whenever he saw Emperor Gaozu and spoke with him, the audience often ran past the hour-mark—so within the Secretariat they had a saying: "When he goes up to the hall he does not come down—there is He the Elegant."

entries.zh: 琛容止都雅，故時人呼之。
entries.en: Chen's carriage was so polished that the nickname stuck.
entries.literal: Chen's bearing was altogether refined, hence people called him that.

entries.zh: 遷散騎常侍，參禮儀如故。
entries.en: He rose to regular attendant of the discretionary cavalry and kept his ritual duties.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Regular Attendant of the Discretionary Cavalry, sharing in ritual affairs as before.

entries.zh: 謇謇有聞，殊稱所期。
entries.en: So your bold reputation precedes you—exactly as we anticipated.
entries.literal: Your outspoken repute has reached us—quite what we expected.

entries.zh: 但朕有天下四十餘年，公車讜言，見聞聽覽，所陳之事，與卿不異，常欲承用，無替懷抱，每苦倥傯，更增惛惑。
entries.en: Yet I have ruled more than forty years. Memorials from the remonstrance office, everything brought to my ears—your complaints are nothing new. I have long meant to act on them and hold to that resolve, but am crushed by daily urgency and only grow more bewildered.
entries.literal: But I have held the realm for forty-odd years; remonstrances from the carriage of petition, all that has reached my hearing and sight—the matters you state do not differ. I have often wished to adopt them and not betray my intent, yet am tormented by pressing affairs and grow only the more confused.

entries.zh: 卿珥貂紆組，博問洽聞，不宜同於郤茸，止取名字，宣之行路。
entries.en: You bear high rank and wide learning. You should not be like Xi Rong, collecting a reputation and peddling it in the streets.
entries.literal: You wear the court insignia and gird the ribbons of office, with broad learning and wide hearing—you should not be like Xi Rong, taking only a name and proclaiming it on the road.

entries.zh: 言「我能上事，明言得失，恨朝廷之不能用」。
entries.en: Boasting, "I can remonstrate and lay bare what is right and wrong, and I resent that the court will not heed me."
entries.literal: Saying, "I can submit affairs and speak clearly of gain and loss, and I resent that the court cannot use me."

entries.zh: 或誦《離騷》「蕩蕩其無人，遂不禦乎千里」。
entries.en: Or quoting the "Li Sao": "Far and wide, no true man—so the chariot will not travel a thousand li."
entries.literal: Or reciting from the "Encountering Sorrow": "Vast and empty—no one there; so he will not drive a thousand li."

entries.zh: 或誦《老子》「知我者希，則我貴矣」。
entries.en: Or quoting the Laozi: "Few know me, and therefore I am honored."
entries.literal: Or reciting from the Laozi: "Those who know me are few, and so I am prized."

entries.zh: 如是獻替，莫不能言，正旦虎樽，皆其人也。
entries.en: Such counsel is cheap; everyone can mouth it. The tiger goblet at New Year—that whole crowd.
entries.literal: Such remonstrance and replacement—everyone can talk; the New Year tiger goblet—the lot of them.

entries.zh: 卿可分別言事，啓乃心，沃朕心。
entries.en: Name your charges one by one. Open your heart and refresh mine.
entries.literal: You should speak of affairs item by item, open your heart, and water my heart.

entries.zh: 普通五年，大舉北伐，魏徐州刺史元法僧遣使請舉地內屬，詔有司議其虛實。
entries.en: In Putong year five the court mounted a major northern campaign; Yuan Faseng, Wei governor of Xuzhou, sent envoys to offer his province in submission, and the throne ordered officials to test the offer’s sincerity.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Putong a great northern expedition was launched; Yuan Faseng, Wei governor of Xuzhou, sent envoys offering to surrender his territory and submit to the dynasty, and an edict ordered the relevant offices to judge whether the offer was genuine.

entries.zh: 异曰：「自王師北討，剋獲相繼，徐州地轉削弱，咸願歸罪法僧，法僧懼禍之至，其降必非偽也。」
entries.en: Yi argued: "Ever since our northern campaigns began, triumph has piled on triumph; Xuzhou weakens daily, and everyone wants to blame Faseng—so, terrified of ruin, he cannot be faking his surrender."
entries.literal: Yi said: "Since our armies marched north, victories have followed one after another; the land of Xuzhou grows ever weaker, and all wish to lay the blame on Faseng. Faseng, fearing disaster, will surely not feign surrender."

entries.zh: 高祖仍遣异報法僧，並敕衆軍應接，受异節度。
entries.en: The emperor dispatched Yi to answer Faseng and directed the field armies to cooperate, all under Yi’s direction.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor then sent Yi to reply to Faseng and also ordered the armies to support him, placing them under Yi’s command.

entries.zh: 旣至，法僧遵承朝旨，如异策焉。
entries.en: On arrival Yi found Faseng obeying the court’s orders exactly as he had predicted.
entries.literal: When Yi arrived, Faseng followed the court’s instructions just as Yi had foreseen.

entries.zh: 大同四年，遷右衛將軍。
entries.en: In Datong 4, Yi was promoted to General of the Right Guard.
entries.literal: In Datong 4, Yi was promoted to General of the Right Guard.

entries.zh: 六年，异啓於儀賢堂奉述高祖《老子義》，敕許之。
entries.en: In the sixth year, Yi petitioned to reverently expound Gaozu's Meaning of the Laozi in Yixian Hall, and an edict permitted it.
entries.literal: In the sixth year, Yi petitioned to reverently expound Gaozu's Meaning of the Laozi in Yixian Hall, and an edict permitted it.

entries.zh: 及就講，朝士及道俗聽者千餘人，爲一時之盛。
entries.en: When he began the lectures, more than a thousand court officials, Daoists, and laypeople came to listen, making it a grand event of the time.
entries.literal: When he began the lectures, more than a thousand court officials, Daoists, and laypeople came to listen, making it a grand event of the time.

entries.zh: 時城西又開士林館以延學士，异與左丞賀琛遞日述高祖《禮記中庸義》，皇太子又召异於玄圃講《易》。
entries.en: At the time, the Shilin Hall west of the city was also opened to host scholars. Yi and Left Assistant Director He Chen took turns by day expounding Gaozu's Meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean in the Book of Rites, and the crown prince also summoned Yi to Xuanpu to lecture on the Changes.
entries.literal: At the time, the Shilin Hall west of the city was also opened to host scholars. Yi and Left Assistant Director He Chen took turns by day expounding Gaozu's Meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean in the Book of Rites, and the crown prince also summoned Yi to Xuanpu to lecture on the Changes.

entries.zh: 八年，改加侍中。
entries.en: In the eighth year, he was changed and additionally made Attendant-in-Ordinary.
entries.literal: In the eighth year, he was changed and additionally made Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 太清元年，遷左衛將軍，領步兵。
entries.en: In Taiqing 1, he was transferred to General of the Left Guard, concurrently Infantry Colonel.
entries.literal: In Taiqing 1, he was transferred to General of the Left Guard, concurrently Infantry Colonel.

entries.zh: 二年，遷中領軍，舍人如故。
entries.en: In the second year, he was transferred to Central Leader of the Army, keeping his post as Secretariat Drafter as before.
entries.literal: In the second year, he was transferred to Central Leader of the Army, keeping his post as Secretariat Drafter as before.

entries.zh: 高祖夢中原平，舉朝稱慶，旦以語异，异對曰：「此宇內方一之征。」
entries.en: The emperor dreamed the north was pacified; courtiers rejoiced. At dawn he told Yi, who answered, "It foretells the unification of the empire."
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor dreamed that the Central Plains were pacified; the whole court offered congratulations. At dawn he told Yi, and Yi replied: "This is a sign that the realm will be united."

entries.zh: 及侯景歸降，敕召羣臣議，尚書僕射謝舉等以爲不可，高祖欲納之，未決；
entries.en: When Hou Jing came in with a surrender offer, the court was convoked to debate; Vice Director Xie Ju and others opposed acceptance, while the emperor leaned toward yes but could not settle his mind;
entries.literal: When Hou Jing offered to surrender, an edict summoned the ministers to debate; Vice Director of the Secretariat Xie Ju and others held that it should not be accepted, while the Founding Emperor wished to agree but had not decided;

entries.zh: 嘗夙興至武德閣，自言「我國家承平若此，今便受地，詎是事宜，脫致紛紜，悔無所及」。
entries.en: one dawn he went early to Wude Pavilion and murmured, "The realm has known such peace—if we take his lands now, is that wise? Once disorder starts, regret will come too late."
entries.literal: once he rose early and went to Wude Pavilion, saying to himself, "Our state has enjoyed peace like this—if we now take his territory, is it really fitting? Should turmoil follow, there will be no place for regret."

entries.zh: 异探高祖微旨，應聲答曰：「聖明御宇，上應蒼玄，北土遺黎，誰不慕仰？
entries.en: Reading the emperor’s mind, Yi answered immediately: "Under your sage rule, answering heaven above, every survivor in the north looks to you with longing—
entries.literal: Yi divined the emperor’s hidden intent and answered at once: "Your sagely rule fills the throne, matching heaven’s dark mystery; the remnant people of the north—who does not look up in longing?

entries.zh: 爲無機會，未達其心。
entries.en: only lacking the chance to reach you.
entries.literal: Only for lack of opportunity have they not yet reached your heart.

entries.zh: 今侯景分魏國太半，輸誠送款，遠歸聖朝，豈非天誘其衷，人獎其計！
entries.en: Now Hou Jing holds more than half of Wei, brings loyalty and tribute, and returns to the sacred court—is this not heaven inclining his heart and men rewarding his design?
entries.literal: Now Hou Jing splits more than half of Wei and offers sincerity and tribute, returning from afar to the holy court—is this not heaven opening his breast and men praising his plan!

entries.zh: 原心審事，殊有可嘉。
entries.en: Weigh motive and fact together, and much deserves praise.
entries.literal: Weigh his intent and examine the matter: there is much to commend.

entries.zh: 今若不容，恐絕後來之望。
entries.en: Reject him now and you may extinguish the hopes of all who would follow.
entries.literal: If you do not accept him now, I fear you will cut off the hopes of those who come after.

entries.zh: 此誠易見，願陛下無疑。」
entries.en: The point is plain; I pray Your Majesty will not hesitate."
entries.literal: This is easy to see; I beg Your Majesty to harbor no doubt."

entries.zh: 高祖深納异言，又感前夢，遂納之。
entries.en: The emperor embraced Yi’s counsel, remembered his dream, and accepted Hou Jing.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor took Yi’s words deeply to heart, was moved as well by his earlier dream, and accepted the surrender.

entries.zh: 及貞陽敗沒，自魏遣使還，述魏相高澄欲更申和睦。
entries.en: After Prince Zhenyang fell into Wei hands, messengers returned saying Chancellor Gao Cheng wished to restore peace.
entries.literal: When Zhenyang was captured and lost, envoys returned from Wei reporting that Chancellor Gao Cheng wished to renew friendly relations.

entries.zh: 敕有司定議，异又以和爲允，高祖果從之。
entries.en: The throne ordered deliberation; Yi again favored peace, and the emperor agreed.
entries.literal: An edict ordered the offices to decide; Yi again judged peace acceptable, and the Founding Emperor followed him.

entries.zh: 其年六月，遣建康令謝挺、通直郎徐陵使北通好。
entries.en: That sixth month he sent Jiankang magistrate Xie Ting and direct attendant Xu Ling north to negotiate amity.
entries.literal: In the sixth month of that year he sent Xie Ting, Magistrate of Jiankang, and Xu Ling, Direct Attendant, north to treat for peace.

entries.zh: 是時，侯景鎮壽春，累啓絕和，及請追使。
entries.en: Hou Jing, then at Shouchun, repeatedly petitioned to sever relations and recall the mission.
entries.literal: At that time Hou Jing was stationed at Shouchun and repeatedly memorialized to break off relations and to recall the envoys.

entries.zh: 又致書與异，辭意甚切，异但述敕旨以報之。
entries.en: He wrote to Yi as well, his tone sharp; Yi answered solely by citing the emperor’s orders.
entries.literal: He also wrote to Yi in very urgent terms; Yi only relayed the wording of the edict in reply.

entries.zh: 八月，景遂舉兵反，以討异爲名。
entries.en: In the eighth month Hou Jing rebelled, naming his cause the punishment of Zhu Yi.
entries.literal: In the eighth month Jing raised troops in revolt, taking "punishing Yi" as his slogan.

entries.zh: 募兵得三千人，及景至，仍以其衆守大司馬門。
entries.en: Yi mustered three thousand men and, when Hou Jing came, still held the Grand Marshal’s gate with them.
entries.literal: He raised three thousand men, and when Jing arrived Yi still used that force to hold the Gate of the Grand Marshal.

entries.zh: 初，景謀反，合州刺史鄱陽王範、司州刺史羊鴉仁並累有啓聞，异以景孤立寄命，必不應爾，乃謂使者：「鄱陽王遂不許國家有一客！」
entries.en: Before the revolt, Prince Fan of Poyang and Governor Yang Yarén of Si had sent repeated warnings; Yi, believing Hou Jing isolated and clinging to the court’s protection, would never dare rebel, told their couriers, "The Prince of Poyang will not even let the state keep one guest!"
entries.literal: Earlier, when Jing plotted rebellion, Prince of Poyang Fan, Governor of He Province, and Yang Yarén, Governor of Si Province, had repeatedly memorialized warning of it; Yi, thinking Jing isolated and dependent on the court’s mercy, would surely not act so, told the messengers: "The Prince of Poyang simply will not let the state keep a single guest!"

entries.zh: 並抑而不奏，故朝廷不爲之備。
entries.en: And buried their reports, so the capital was caught unprepared.
entries.literal: and suppressed the memorials without forwarding them, so the court made no preparations.

entries.zh: 及寇至，城內文武咸尤之。
entries.en: When the enemy reached the walls, every official inside the city reproached him.
entries.literal: When the invader reached the city, civil and military officials within the walls all blamed him.

entries.zh: 皇太子又制《圍城賦》，其末章云：「彼高冠及厚履，並鼎食而乘肥，升紫霄之丹地，排玉殿之金扉，陳謀謨之啓沃，宣政刑之福威，四郊以之多壘，萬邦以之未綏。
entries.en: The crown prince wrote the "Rhapsody on the Besieged City," whose final lines run: "They of high caps and thick soles, feasting on rich fare and riding plump horses, climb the scarlet courts of purple heaven and thrust open the golden gates of jade halls—counseling at the inner audience, wielding the blessings and terrors of law—till the suburbs bristle with ramparts and the realm knows no rest.
entries.literal: The Crown Prince also composed the "Rhapsody on Besieging the City"; its closing section reads: "Those with high caps and thick shoes, all feasting richly and riding fat steeds, ascend the cinnabar ground of purple heaven and push open the golden doors of jade halls, presenting counsel at the inner court and proclaiming the blessings and terrors of government and punishment—so the four suburbs grow many ramparts and the myriad states know no peace.

entries.zh: 問豺狼其何者？
entries.en: Who are the wolves and jackals?
entries.literal: Ask: which are the wolves and jackals?

entries.zh: 訪虺蜴之爲誰？」
entries.en: Who are the vipers and basilisks?"
entries.literal: Inquire: who are the venomous snakes and lizards?"

entries.zh: 蓋以指异。
entries.en: The lines plainly targeted Yi.
entries.literal: This was plainly aimed at Yi.

entries.zh: 异因慚憤，發病卒，時年六十七。
entries.en: Stung by shame and anger, Yi took ill and died at sixty-seven.
entries.literal: Yi, shamed and enraged, fell ill and died, aged sixty-seven.

entries.zh: 詔曰：「故中領軍异，器宇弘通，才力優贍，諮謀帷幄，多歷年所。
entries.en: The edict read: "The late Central Commander-in-Chief Yi bore a great and open mind and ample talent; for years he counseled within the command tent.
entries.literal: The edict said: "The late Central Commander-in-Chief Yi possessed a broad and penetrating capacity and abundant talent and strength; for many years he advised within the curtain of state.

entries.zh: 方贊朝經，永申寄任。
entries.en: He was to have upheld the court’s order and long borne our commission.
entries.literal: He was just assisting the court’s institutions and would long have carried our trust.

entries.zh: 奄先物化，惻悼兼懷。
entries.en: Suddenly he left the world, and our sorrow is twofold.
entries.literal: Suddenly he passed from among the living; our grief is doubled.

entries.zh: 可贈侍中、尚書右僕射，給秘器一具。
entries.en: Let him be mourned as Palace Attendant and Right Vice Director of the Secretariat, with one set of secret burial vessels.
entries.literal: He may be posthumously awarded Palace Attendant and Right Vice Director of the Secretariat, with one set of secret burial vessels granted.

entries.zh: 凶事所須，隨由資辦。」
entries.en: All funeral needs are to be furnished as required."
entries.literal: Whatever the funeral requires shall be supplied as needed."

entries.zh: 舊尚書官不以爲贈，及异卒，高祖惜之，方議贈事。
entries.en: Formerly secretariat posts were not granted posthumously; when Yi died the emperor grieved and debated what honor to give.
entries.literal: By old custom ministerial offices were not given as posthumous titles; when Yi died the Founding Emperor regretted it and was just then debating the award.

entries.zh: 左右有善异者，乃啓曰：「异忝曆雖多，然平生所懷，願得執法。」
entries.en: An attendant who admired Yi submitted: "For all his long service, his lifelong wish was to wield the law."
entries.literal: A courtier who favored Yi then memorialized: "Though Yi’s years of service were many, what he cherished all his life was to hold the law."

entries.zh: 高祖因其宿志，特有此贈焉。
entries.en: Honoring that lifelong wish, the emperor granted this exceptional title.
entries.literal: The Founding Emperor, honoring his old wish, made this special grant.

entries.zh: 書奏，高祖大怒，召主書於前，口授敕責琛曰：
entries.en: The memorial was read; Gaozu flew into a rage, called the chief clerk to his side, and dictated a rebuke to Chen:
entries.literal: When the memorial was submitted, Gaozu was greatly angered; he summoned the chief clerk before him and orally dictated an edict rebuking Chen, saying:

entries.zh: 卿云「今北邊稽服，政是生聚教訓之時，而民失安居，牧守之過」。
entries.en: You wrote: "The north has submitted. This should be a time to let the people settle and thrive, yet they cannot live in peace—that is the fault of local officials."
entries.literal: You say, "Now the north submits—this is precisely the time to gather and teach the people, yet they lose peaceful dwelling; the fault lies with the governors."

entries.zh: 朕無則哲之知，觸向多弊，四聰不開，四明不達，內省責躬，無處逃咎。
entries.en: I am no sage of discernment. I stumble into wrong after wrong. My ears and eyes do not reach everywhere. I blame only myself and cannot escape that blame.
entries.literal: I lack knowing discernment; I touch on many abuses; the four hearers are unopened and the four seeers unreached—inwardly I examine and blame myself, with nowhere to flee guilt.

entries.zh: 堯爲聖主，四凶在朝；
entries.en: Yao was a sage, and still the Four Evils sat in court;
entries.literal: Yao was a sage lord, yet the four villains were in court;

entries.zh: 況乎朕也，能無惡人？
entries.en: how then can I, of all men, have none?
entries.literal: how much more I—can there be no wicked men?

entries.zh: 但大澤之中，有龍有蛇，縱不盡善，不容皆惡。
entries.en: A great marsh holds dragons and snakes alike. Not every officer is worthy, but not every one is corrupt.
entries.literal: But in a great marsh there are dragons and snakes; though not all are good, not all can be wicked.

entries.zh: 卿可分明顯出：某刺史橫暴，某太守貪殘，某官長凶虐；
entries.en: Name them plainly: which governor is brutal, which prefect greedy and cruel, which magistrate savage;
entries.literal: You may clearly name them: such-and-such a governor is violent, such-and-such a prefect greedy and cruel, such-and-such a chief brutal;

entries.zh: 尚書、蘭臺，主書、舍人，某人姦猾，某人取與，明言其事，得以黜陟。
entries.en: which minister, which Orchid Terrace clerk, which recorder or attendant is crooked or on the take. State the facts and they can be promoted or removed.
entries.literal: which minister or Orchid Terrace clerk, which chief clerk or attendant, is crafty, which takes bribes—state the matter clearly so dismissal and promotion may follow.

entries.zh: 向令舜但聽公車上書，四凶終自不知，堯亦永爲暗主。
entries.en: If Shun had listened only to anonymous memorials, the Four Evils would never have been exposed and Yao would have remained a blind ruler forever.
entries.literal: Had Shun only listened to memorials on the carriage of remonstrance, the four villains would never have been known, and Yao would forever have been a dim ruler.

entries.zh: 卿又云「東境戶口空虛，良由使命繁多」，但未知此是何使？
entries.en: You also say, "The east is depopulated because envoys are too many." Which envoys do you mean?
entries.literal: You also say, "The eastern marches' households are empty, truly because missions are numerous"—but which missions are these?

entries.zh: 卿云「駑困邑宰，則拱手聽其漁獵；
entries.en: You say, "Weak magistrates can only stand by while others plunder;
entries.literal: You say, "When incompetent district chiefs are worn down, they fold their hands while others fish and hunt;

entries.zh: 桀黠長吏，又因之而爲貪殘」，並何姓名？
entries.en: and crafty senior officials use the chance to grow greedier still." Who are they? Name them.
entries.literal: "crafty senior officials further use this to be greedy and cruel"—what are their names?

entries.zh: 廉平掣肘，復是何人？
entries.en: And who are the upright officials being blocked?
entries.literal: Who are the honest and fair yet hamstrung?

entries.zh: 朝廷思賢，有如饑渴，廉平掣肘，實爲異事。
entries.en: The throne seeks worthy men as a thirsty man seeks water. That the honest should be obstructed would be extraordinary.
entries.literal: The court thirsts for the worthy as for hunger and thirst—honest men hamstrung is truly a strange thing.

entries.zh: 宜速條聞，當更擢用。
entries.en: List them at once. We will promote them without delay.
entries.literal: Quickly itemize and report; they shall be promoted and employed anew.

entries.zh: 凡所遣使，多由民訟，或復軍糧，諸所飆急，蓋不獲已而遣之。
entries.en: Most missions answer lawsuits or move army grain. Urgent business leaves little choice but to send men.
entries.literal: Most envoys sent are for the people's lawsuits, or again for army grain; urgencies everywhere—mostly they are sent with no choice.

entries.zh: 若不遣使，天下枉直云何綜理？
entries.en: Without envoys, how is justice to be done across the land?
entries.literal: If envoys are not sent, how are right and wrong across the realm to be sorted?

entries.zh: 事實云何濟辦？
entries.en: How is real business to get done?
entries.literal: How are facts to be accomplished?

entries.zh: 惡人日滋，善人日蔽，欲求安臥，其可得乎！
entries.en: Villains multiply by the day while the good are shut out. Do you imagine the realm can then rest easy?
entries.literal: Wicked men daily multiply, good men daily eclipsed—wish to lie at ease: can this be obtained?

entries.zh: 不遣使而得事理，此乃佳事。
entries.en: To govern without envoys and still set everything right—that would be splendid.
entries.literal: Not to send envoys yet gain orderly affairs—this would be excellent.

entries.zh: 無足而行，無翼而飛，能到在所；
entries.en: Feet that need not walk, wings that need not beat, yet arrival everywhere;
entries.literal: To walk without feet, fly without wings, and reach wherever needed;

entries.zh: 不威而伏，豈不幸甚。
entries.en: obedience without coercion—what could be more fortunate?
entries.literal: to submit without awe—would that not be greatly fortunate.

entries.zh: 卿旣言之，應有深見，宜陳秘術，不可懷寶迷邦。
entries.en: You have raised the matter, so you must know the remedy. Reveal your secret art. Do not hide wisdom and leave the realm in the dark.
entries.literal: Since you have spoken thus, you must have deep insight; proclaim the secret method—do not hoard treasure and mislead the state.

entries.zh: 普通中，刺史臨川王辟爲祭酒從事史。
entries.en: During Putong the Prince of Linchuan, as inspector, took him on as libationer and clerk.
entries.literal: In the Putong era the Prince of Linchuan, as regional inspector, engaged him as Libationer and Clerk.

entries.zh: 琛始出都，高祖聞其學術，召見文德殿，與語悅之，謂僕射徐勉曰：「琛殊有世業。」
entries.en: On first reaching the capital Chen was summoned to Wende Hall; the emperor, pleased by their talk, told Vice Director Xu Mian, "Chen indeed inherits a scholarly house."
entries.literal: When Chen first came to the capital the Founding Emperor, hearing of his learning, summoned him to Wende Hall; speaking with him, the emperor was pleased and said to Vice Director Xu Mian: "Chen truly carries on a family tradition."

entries.zh: 仍補王國侍郎，俄兼太學博士，稍遷中衛參軍事、尚書通事舍人，參禮儀事。
entries.en: He was made a gentleman of the prince’s establishment, then imperial academy erudite, and rose to central guard army aide and secretariat attendant, sharing in ritual matters.
entries.literal: He was then appointed Gentleman of the Prince’s Kingdom, soon added as Erudite of the Imperial Academy, and gradually promoted to Army Aide in the Central Guard and Secretariat Attendant, taking part in ritual affairs.

entries.zh: 累遷通直正員郎，舍人如故。
entries.en: He advanced to direct attendant with regular rank while keeping his attendant post.
entries.literal: He was promoted in succession to Direct Attendant with regular rank, retaining his post as Attendant.

entries.zh: 又征西鄱陽王中錄事，兼尚書左丞，滿歲爲真。
entries.en: He also served as recorder to the Western Expedition Prince of Poyang and concurrently left assistant director of the Secretariat, confirmed in the latter after a year.
entries.literal: He was also Recorder to the Western Expedition Prince of Poyang, concurrently Left Assistant Director of the Secretariat, and after a full year was confirmed in the latter post.

entries.zh: 詔琛撰《新諡法》，至今施用。
entries.en: The throne ordered him to draft the "New Method of Posthumous Titles," still applied today.
entries.literal: An edict ordered Chen to compile the "New Method of Posthumous Titles," which is still in use today.

entries.zh: 是時，高祖任職者，皆緣飾姦諂，深害時政，琛遂啓陳事條封奏曰：
entries.en: By then every man in power under Gaozu trimmed his conduct with flattery and fraud, corroding government; Chen submitted a sealed memorial, item by item, saying:
entries.literal: At that time those in office under Gaozu all adorned themselves in flattery and deceit, deeply harming current policy; Chen therefore memorialized, setting forth matters item by item in a sealed memorial, saying:

entries.zh: 臣荷拔擢之恩，曾不能效一職；
entries.en: I have enjoyed Your Majesty's favor yet rendered no service worthy of a single post;
entries.literal: Your subject has received the grace of elevation yet has never been able to serve in a single office worthily;

entries.zh: 居獻納之任，又不能薦一言。
entries.en: I hold a remonstrance office yet have not offered one loyal word.
entries.literal: holding the post of presentation and remonstrance, yet unable to offer a single word of recommendation.

entries.zh: 竊聞「慈父不愛無益之子，明君不畜無益之臣」，臣所以當食廢飧，中宵而歎息也。
entries.en: I know that "a loving father keeps no useless son, a wise ruler keeps no useless minister"—and so I lose my appetite and sigh through the night.
entries.literal: I have heard that "a loving father does not keep a useless son, an enlightened ruler does not keep a useless minister"—for this reason I cannot finish my meals and sigh in the middle of the night.

entries.zh: 輒言時事，列之於後。
entries.en: I venture to set out the times, point by point below.
entries.literal: I venture to speak of current affairs, listing them below.

entries.zh: 非謂謀猷，寧云啓沃。
entries.en: This is not polished counsel, only an honest opening of the heart.
entries.literal: I do not mean to offer strategy, but simply to open and nourish.

entries.zh: 獨緘胸臆，不語妻子。
entries.en: I have locked it in my breast and told neither wife nor child.
entries.literal: I alone seal it in my breast and do not speak of it even to wife and children.

entries.zh: 辭無粉飾，削槁則焚。
entries.en: My words are unadorned; if they are rejected I will burn the draft.
entries.literal: My words have no ornament; if they are cut down to bare stalk I will burn them.

entries.zh: 脫得聽覽，試加省鑒。
entries.en: If Your Majesty will read them, please weigh them yourself.
entries.literal: If I may obtain Your Majesty's reading, please try to examine them.

entries.zh: 如不允合，亮其戇愚。
entries.en: If they miss the mark, bear with my blunt folly.
entries.literal: If they do not meet approval, forgive my blunt foolishness.

entries.zh: 其二事曰：聖主恤隱之心，納隍之念，聞之遐邇，至於翾飛蠕動，猶且度脫，況在兆庶。
entries.en: Second: the sage ruler's pity for the suffering and his will to save the drowning reach the four quarters—even insects he would spare, how much more the people.
entries.literal: The second matter says: The sage lord's heart of pity for the hidden, and the thought of receiving the drowning in the moat, are heard far and near—even flying insects and wriggling creatures he would still deliver—how much more the myriad people.

entries.zh: 而州郡無恤民之志，故天下顒顒，惟注仰於一人，誠所謂「愛之如父母，仰之如日月，敬之如鬼神，畏之如雷霆」。
entries.en: Yet provinces and commanderies show no care for the people, so the realm fixes its hope on Your Majesty alone—as the saying has it, "loving you as parents, looking up as to sun and moon, revering you as spirits, fearing you as thunder."
entries.literal: Yet provinces and commanderies lack the will to comfort the people, so all under heaven look up expectantly to one man alone—truly what is called "loving him as parents, looking up to him as sun and moon, revering him as spirits, fearing him as thunder."

entries.zh: 苟須應痛逗藥，豈可不治之哉？
entries.en: When the body aches, medicine must follow—how can the sickness go untreated?
entries.literal: If medicine must be applied where there is pain, how can one fail to treat it?

entries.zh: 今天下宰守所以皆尚貪殘，罕有廉白者，良由風俗侈靡。
entries.en: Today magistrates and governors are greedy and cruel, rarely honest—because extravagant custom drives them to it.
entries.literal: Today all the realm's magistrates and guardians for this reason mostly prize greed and cruelty, rarely being clean and white—truly it is the custom of extravagant display that makes them so.

entries.zh: 使之然也。
entries.en: Luxury makes them so.
entries.literal: that makes them so.

entries.zh: 淫奢之弊，其事多端，粗舉二條，言其尤者。
entries.en: Extravagance has many faces; I name two of the worst.
entries.literal: The abuses of wanton luxury have many aspects; I roughly offer two items, speaking of the chief ones.

entries.zh: 夫食方丈于前，所甘一味。
entries.en: Before a table ten feet across, the tongue savors only one taste.
entries.literal: Before a table ten feet square, what the palate delights in is but one flavor.

entries.zh: 今之燕喜，相競誇豪，積果如山嶽，列肴同綺繡，露臺之產，不周一燕之資，而賓主之間，裁取滿腹，未及下堂，已同臭腐。
entries.en: Today's feasts compete in display—fruit heaped like hills, dishes laid like brocade; a terrace garden's yield cannot pay for one banquet, yet host and guest eat only their fill and leave the rest to rot before they quit the hall.
entries.literal: Today's banquets vie in boasting extravagance—fruit piled like mountains, dishes spread like brocade; the yield of a terrace garden does not suffice for one feast's cost, while between host and guest they take only a full belly—before leaving the hall it is already like rotting stench.

entries.zh: 又歌姬儛女，本有品制，二八之錫，良待和戎。
entries.en: Courtesans and dancers once had fixed ranks; the "two eight" maidens were reserved for pacifying barbarians.
entries.literal: Again, singing girls and dancing women originally had their grades; the gift of "two eights" was truly reserved for harmonizing with the barbarians.

entries.zh: 今畜妓之夫，無有等秩，雖復庶賤微人，皆盛姬薑，務在貪污，爭飾羅綺。
entries.en: Today men who keep women observe no rank—even the humblest pack their houses with concubines, greedy for graft, vying in silk and finery.
entries.literal: Today men who keep courtesans have no rank distinction—even humble and lowly men all fill their quarters with beauties, striving in corruption, competing to adorn with silk.

entries.zh: 故爲吏牧民者，競爲剝削，雖致貲巨億，罷歸之日，不支數年，便已消散。
entries.en: Officials who should shepherd the people race to strip them; though they amass tens of millions, a few years after leaving office the fortune is gone.
entries.literal: Therefore those who as officials shepherd the people compete in stripping and cutting; though they amass wealth in the hundreds of millions, by the day they leave office, within a few years it is already dissipated.

entries.zh: 蓋由宴醑所費，旣破數家之產；
entries.en: Banquets alone can ruin several families' worth;
entries.literal: For the cost of banquets and feasts has already ruined several households' property;

entries.zh: 歌謠之具，必俟千金之資。
entries.en: and song and dance demand capital of a thousand gold.
entries.literal: the equipment for songs must wait on capital of a thousand gold.

entries.zh: 所費事等丘山，爲歡止在俄頃。
entries.en: Spending mounts like hills; pleasure lasts a breath.
entries.literal: The outlay equals hills and mountains; the pleasure lasts only an instant.

entries.zh: 乃更追恨向所取之少，今所費之多。
entries.en: Then they regret having taken too little before and spending too much now.
entries.literal: Then they further regret that what they took before was little and what they spend now is much.

entries.zh: 如復傅翼，增其搏噬，一何悖哉！
entries.en: Give them wings again and they tear all the harder—how perverse!
entries.literal: If they are given wings again, to increase their tearing and devouring—how perverse!

entries.zh: 其餘淫侈，著之凡百，習以成俗，日見滋甚，欲使人守廉隅，吏尚清白，安可得邪！
entries.en: Other luxuries fill a hundred lists; habit deepens daily—how can we ask men to stay honest and officials to stay clean?
entries.literal: The rest of wanton excess is written in a hundred particulars; habit becomes custom and daily grows worse—wishing men to keep clean corners and officials to honor whiteness, how can it be obtained!

entries.zh: 今誠宜嚴爲禁制，道之以節儉，貶黜雕飾，糾奏浮華，使衆皆知，變其耳目，改其好惡。
entries.en: Impose stern bans, teach frugality, demote ornament, impeach showy waste, until all see it and change what they desire.
entries.literal: Now one should truly impose stern prohibitions, guide them with frugality, demote carved ornament, memorialize and impeach floating display, so that all know it and change what their eyes and ears take in, change what they love and hate.

entries.zh: 夫失節之嗟，亦民所自患，正恥不及羣，故勉強而爲之，苟力所不至，還受其弊矣。
entries.en: People too regret excess—they only fear falling behind the crowd and force themselves on; when they cannot keep up, they still bear the cost.
entries.literal: The sigh at loss of restraint is also what the people themselves worry over—they are just ashamed not to match the crowd, so they force themselves to do it; if their strength does not reach, they still suffer the harm.

entries.zh: 今若厘其風而正其失，易於反掌。
entries.en: Correct the wind and the fault rights itself—easier than turning the hand.
entries.literal: Now if one corrects the wind and rights the faults, it is easier than turning the palm.

entries.zh: 夫論至治者，必以淳素爲先，正雕流之弊，莫有過儉樸者也。
entries.en: Supreme rule begins in plain simplicity; to cure ornamental excess nothing beats thrift.
entries.literal: In discussing supreme governance one must take plain simplicity first; in correcting the abuses of carved display nothing surpasses plain frugality.

entries.zh: 其三事曰：聖躬荷負蒼生以爲任，弘濟四海以爲心，不憚胼胝之勞，不辭臒瘦之苦，豈止日昃忘饑，夜分廢寢。
entries.en: Third: Your Majesty bears the people's weight and takes the four seas to heart, unafraid of toil that callouses hand and foot or hardship that wastes the flesh—forgetting hunger as the sun sets and sleep at midnight.
entries.literal: The third matter says: The sacred person bears the burden of the dark-haired people as his charge, takes succoring the four seas as his heart, does not shrink from the labor of calloused hands and feet, does not decline the suffering of emaciation—how much more forgetting hunger as the sun declines and abandoning sleep at midnight.

entries.zh: 至於百司，莫不奏事，上息責下之嫌，下無逼上之咎，斯實道邁百王，事超千載。
entries.en: Every office may memorialize; above, no blame for pressing down, below, no fault for pressing up—a government surpassing a hundred kings.
entries.literal: As for the hundred offices, none fail to memorialize; above rests the blame of pressing down, below there is no fault of pressing up—truly the Way surpasses a hundred kings, affairs exceed a thousand ages.

entries.zh: 但鬥筲之人，藻棁之子，旣得伏奏帷扆，便欲詭競求進，不說國之大體。
entries.en: Yet petty men, once they may speak behind the curtain, scheme for promotion and never speak for the realm's whole design.
entries.literal: But petty-vessel men, chopstick-sized talents, once allowed to memorialize behind the curtain, at once wish to compete deviously for advancement, not speaking of the state's great structure.

entries.zh: 不知當一官，處一職，貴使理其紊亂，匡其不及，心在明恕，事乃平章。
entries.en: They forget that each post exists to set disorder right and mend what is lacking—with a heart of clarity and forbearance, affairs find their balance.
entries.literal: They do not know that holding one office and filling one post means it is noble to put order to its disorder and remedy its shortfalls—the heart dwelling in clear forbearance, affairs then balanced and measured.

entries.zh: 但務吹毛求疵，擘肌分理，運挈瓶之智，徼分外之求，以深刻爲能，以繩逐爲務，跡雖似於奉公，事更成其威福。
entries.en: They split hairs, split hairs again, wield petty cleverness, grasp beyond their share, prize harshness and chase by the letter—seeming dutiful while building private power.
entries.literal: They only pursue splitting hairs for flaws, splitting muscle to distinguish principle, wielding the wisdom of carrying a bottle, seeking reward beyond their portion, taking severity as ability and driving by the cord as their task—traces seem to serve the public, but affairs more build their authority and blessings.

entries.zh: 犯罪者多，巧避滋甚，曠官廢職，長弊增姦，實由於此。
entries.en: Crime multiplies, evasion grows clever, posts empty and duties rot—long corruption and fresh treachery spring from this.
entries.literal: The criminal are many, clever evasion grows worse, offices lie vacant and duties abandoned, long abuses and mounting treachery—truly spring from this.

entries.zh: 今誠願責其公平之效，黜其讒愚之心，則下安上謐，無僥倖之患矣。
entries.en: Demand fair results, purge slanderous hearts—then the lower ranks rest, the throne is secure, and lucky scheming ends.
entries.literal: Now one truly ought to demand the effect of their fairness, dismiss their slanderous foolish hearts—then below is settled and above is quiet, without the worry of lucky chance.

entries.zh: 其四事曰：自征伐北境，帑藏空虛。
entries.en: Fourth: northern campaigns have emptied the treasury.
