entries.literal: The fourth matter says: From campaigns on the northern frontier, the treasury stores stand empty.

entries.zh: 今天下無事，而猶日不暇給者，良有以也。
entries.en: The realm is at peace, yet you have no leisure day by day—and there is reason.
entries.literal: Today the realm is without affairs, yet there is still no leisure day after day—there is good reason.

entries.zh: 夫國弊則省其事而息其費，事省則養民，費息則財聚，止五年之中，尚於無事，必能使國豊民阜。
entries.en: When the state is strained, cut tasks and spending; fewer tasks nurture the people, less spending piles wealth—in five years of peace the realm can grow rich.
entries.literal: When the state is exhausted, reduce its affairs and rest its expenditures; when affairs are reduced the people are nurtured, when expenditures rest wealth gathers—in within five years, while still without affairs, one can surely make the state rich and the people prosperous.

entries.zh: 若積以歲月，斯乃范蠡滅吳之術，管仲霸齊之由。
entries.en: Sustained over years, this is how Fan Li destroyed Wu and Guan Zhong made Qi hegemon.
entries.literal: If this accumulates over months and years, this is the method by which Fan Li destroyed Wu, the reason Guan Zhong made Qi hegemon.

entries.zh: 今應內省職掌，各檢其所部。
entries.en: Examine each office inwardly; let every department audit its own charge.
entries.literal: Now one ought inwardly to examine offices' charge, each inspecting what their department does.

entries.zh: 凡京師治、署、邸、肆應所爲，或十條宜省其五，或三條宜除其一；
entries.en: In the capital—bureaus, offices, lodges, markets—of ten duties cut five, or of three cut one;
entries.literal: As for all in the capital—administration, offices, lodges, markets—that should be done, perhaps of ten items five ought to be cut, or of three items one ought to be removed;

entries.zh: 及國容、戎備，在昔應多，在今宜少。
entries.en: state ceremony and armaments once needed to be many; today they should be few.
entries.literal: and state display and military preparedness—in the past should have been many, today ought to be few.

entries.zh: 雖于後應多，卽事未須，皆悉減省。
entries.en: What future need may bring can wait; what present need does not require—cut it all.
entries.literal: Though afterward more may be needed, what the affair now does not require—all alike reduce and cut.

entries.zh: 應四方屯、傳、邸、治，或舊有，或無益，或妨民，有所宜除，除之；
entries.en: Throughout the realm—garrisons, relays, lodges, offices—whether obsolete, useless, or harmful—abolish what should be abolished;
entries.literal: All around the four quarters—garrison posts, relay stations, lodges, administrations—whether old-established, or useless, or harming the people—what should be removed, remove it;

entries.zh: 有所宜減，減之。
entries.en: trim what should be trimmed.
entries.literal: what should be reduced, reduce it.

entries.zh: 凡厥興造，凡厥費財，有非急者，有役民者；
entries.en: Every project, every outlay of treasure—not urgent, or pressing the people into labor;
entries.literal: All construction, all expenditure of wealth—if not urgent, if conscripting the people;

entries.zh: 又凡厥討召，凡厥徵求，雖關國計，權其事宜，皆須息費休民。
entries.en: Every requisition and levy, however vital to state finance, must be judged on its merits and made to spare the treasury and spare the people.
entries.literal: Further, all summons and all levies—even when they touch the state accounts—must be weighed for fitness; all alike must rest spending and rest the people.

entries.zh: 不息費，則無以聚財；
entries.en: Unless spending is curbed, wealth cannot accumulate;
entries.literal: Without resting expenditure, there is no way to gather wealth;

entries.zh: 不休民，則無以聚力。
entries.en: unless the people are given rest, their strength cannot be gathered.
entries.literal: without resting the people, there is no way to gather strength.

entries.zh: 故蓄其財者，所以大用之也；
entries.en: Wealth is hoarded so it may be spent greatly;
entries.literal: Thus to store wealth is precisely for great use;

entries.zh: 息其民者，所以大役之也。
entries.en: the people are rested so they may bear great toil.
entries.literal: to rest the people is precisely for great labor.

entries.zh: 若言小事不足害財，則終年不息矣；
entries.en: Call waste trivial and spending never stops for a year;
entries.literal: If one says small matters cannot harm wealth, then spending never rests the whole year long;

entries.zh: 以小役不足妨民，則終年不止矣。
entries.en: call corvée slight and conscription never ends for a year.
entries.literal: if one says small corvées cannot hinder the people, then labor never stops the whole year long.

entries.zh: 擾其民而欲求生聚殷阜，不可得矣。
entries.en: Harass the people and expect them to multiply and prosper—that cannot be done.
entries.literal: Harass the people yet wish for growth, gathering, and abundance—this cannot be obtained.

entries.zh: 耗其財而務賦斂繁興，則姦詐盜竊彌生，是弊不息而其民不可使也，則難可以語富強而圖遠大矣。
entries.en: Drain the treasury while heaping up taxes, and deceit and theft flourish; abuses never end and the people cannot be commanded—then there is no talking of power or far-reaching aims.
entries.literal: Exhaust wealth yet pursue frequent levies, and fraud and theft multiply; evils never cease and the people cannot be employed—then it is hard to speak of wealth and strength or plan for the distant and great.

entries.zh: 自普通以來，二十餘年，刑役薦起，民力雕流。
entries.en: For more than twenty years since Putong, penal labor and corvée have surged without pause, and popular strength has been worn to nothing.
entries.literal: Since the Putong era, for twenty-odd years, punishments and corvée have risen again and again, and the people's strength has been carved away and scattered.

entries.zh: 今魏氏和親，疆埸無警，若不及於此時大息四民，使之生聚，減省國費，令府庫蓄積，一旦異境有虞，關河可掃，則國弊民疲，安能振其遠略？
entries.en: The Northern Wei are reconciled and the borders are quiet. Fail now to give the people real rest, let them multiply, cut state expense, and stock the coffers, and when a neighbor turns hostile and the frontier must be held, the realm will already be hollow and the people exhausted—what grand design can you then pursue?
entries.literal: Now the Wei have made peace and the marches are unalarmed; if we do not at this time greatly rest the four classes of people, let them grow and gather, reduce state costs, and fill the treasuries—once another realm grows wary and the passes must be swept clean—then with the state spent and the people weary, how can we rouse a distant strategy?

entries.zh: 事至方圖，知不及矣。
entries.en: Wait until crisis comes to plan, and you will find you are already too late.
entries.literal: To plan only when the affair has arrived is to know that one will be too late.

entries.zh: 卿又云：守宰貪殘，皆由滋味過度。
entries.en: You also say, "Local greed and cruelty all come from extravagant food."
entries.literal: You also say: "Governors' greed and cruelty all come from excessive delicacies."

entries.zh: 貪殘糜費，已如前答。
entries.en: On greed, cruelty, and waste I have already replied.
entries.literal: Greed, cruelty, and wasteful spending—I have already answered as before.

entries.zh: 漢文雖愛露臺之產，鄧通之錢布於天下，以此而治，朕無愧焉。
entries.en: Han Wendi loved his terrace garden and Deng Tong's wealth filled the realm. I rule no worse and feel no shame.
entries.literal: Han Wendi though he loved the terrace crop, Deng Tong's coin spread through the realm—with such governance I have no shame.

entries.zh: 若以下民飲食過差，亦復不然。
entries.en: Nor is it true that commoners eat beyond their station.
entries.literal: As for common people's food overstepping bounds—that too is not so.

entries.zh: 天監之初，思之已甚。
entries.en: I considered this carefully at the beginning of Tianjian.
entries.literal: At the start of Tianjian I thought on this deeply.

entries.zh: 其勤力營產，則無不富饒；
entries.en: Those who work hard prosper;
entries.literal: Those who labor to build property are without exception rich;

entries.zh: 惰游緩事，則家業貧窶。
entries.en: the idle and careless grow poor.
entries.literal: the idle and slack in affairs end in poverty.

entries.zh: 勤修產業，以營盤案，自己營之，自己食之，何損於天下？
entries.en: A man who builds his estate and eats what he earns—how does that harm the realm?
entries.literal: Diligently manage property and set the table—oneself earn it, oneself eat it: what harm to the realm?

entries.zh: 無賴子弟，惰營產業，致於貧窶，無可施設，此何益於天下？
entries.en: Wastrels who neglect their fields end penniless and useless—what good is that to the realm?
entries.literal: Good-for-nothing sons who idly neglect property end in poverty with nothing to deploy—what benefit to the realm?

entries.zh: 且又意雖曰同富，富有不同：慳而富者，終不能設；
entries.en: You speak as if all wealth were the same, but it is not. The miser may be rich yet can do nothing with it;
entries.literal: And though one may speak of "equal wealth," wealth differs: the stingy rich can never deploy;

entries.zh: 奢而富者，于事何損？
entries.en: the spendthrift rich—what injury do they do the state?
entries.literal: the lavish rich—what harm to affairs?

entries.zh: 若使朝廷緩其刑，此事終不可斷；
entries.en: Relax the law and excess will never end;
entries.literal: If the court eases punishments, this can never be ended;

entries.zh: 若急其制，則曲屋密房之中，云何可知？
entries.en: tighten it and who can see what happens behind closed doors?
entries.literal: if it tightens regulation, then inside curved chambers and hidden rooms—how can one know?

entries.zh: 若家家搜檢，其細已甚，欲使吏不呼門，其可得乎？
entries.en: Search every home and the scrutiny becomes unbearable. You want officials never to knock on a door—is that possible?
entries.literal: If every house is searched, the minutiae become extreme—wish clerks never to knock at doors: can this be obtained?

entries.zh: 更相恐脅，以求財帛，足長禍萌，無益治道。
entries.en: Men threatening one another for money only breed worse trouble. That is no way to govern.
entries.literal: Mutual intimidation to extract coin only lengthens the sprouts of disaster and benefits governance not at all.

entries.zh: 若以此指朝廷，我無此事。
entries.en: If you mean the court by this, I know nothing of it.
entries.literal: If by this you mean the court—I have no such matter.

entries.zh: 昔之牲牢，久不宰殺，朝中會同，菜蔬而已，意粗得奢約之節。
entries.en: For years we ceased slaughtering for sacrifice. Court feasts were vegetables only. I thought I had found a fair balance of frugality and dignity.
entries.literal: Formerly sacrificial beasts went long unslaughtered; court gatherings had only vegetables—I roughly grasped the measure of splendor and thrift.

entries.zh: 若復減此，必有《蟋蟀》之譏。
entries.en: Cut more and you will invite the reproach of the "Cricket."
entries.literal: If this is reduced further, there will surely be the reproach of the "Cricket."

entries.zh: 若以爲功德事者，皆是園中之所產育。
entries.en: If you mean Buddhist merit works, their food comes from the palace gardens.
entries.literal: If you think merit affairs—all are bred in the imperial gardens.

entries.zh: 功德之事，亦無多費，變一瓜爲數十種，食一菜爲數十味，不變瓜菜，亦無多種，以變故多，何損於事，亦豪芥不關國家。
entries.en: Even merit feasts cost little. One melon becomes a dozen dishes, one vegetable a dozen flavors—yet without artifice there are few kinds. What harm is there in variety? It does not touch the state at all.
entries.literal: Merit affairs also cost little: one melon into dozens of kinds, one dish into dozens of flavors; without changing melon or vegetable there are not many kinds—because of variety, what harm to affairs? It touches the state not in the least.

entries.zh: 如得財如法而用，此不愧乎人。
entries.en: Wealth lawfully gained and lawfully spent is nothing to be ashamed of.
entries.literal: To obtain wealth and use it lawfully—this is no shame before men.

entries.zh: 我自除公宴，不食國家之食，多歷年稔，乃至宮人，亦不食國家之食，積累歲月。
entries.en: Apart from state banquets I have not eaten public rations for many years, and even the palace women have gone without them for a long time.
entries.literal: I myself, apart from public feasts, do not eat the state's food—many years; even palace women do not eat state food—months piled up.

entries.zh: 凡所營造，不關材官，及以國匠，皆資雇借，以成其事。
entries.en: Every building project avoids the materials bureau and state craftsmen. I hire labor and pay for the work myself.
entries.literal: All construction does not involve the materials office or state artisans—all is hired on loan to complete the work.

entries.zh: 近之得財，頗有方便，民得其利，國得其利，我得其利，營諸功德。
entries.en: Money lately raised has served everyone: the people profit, the state profits, I profit, and merit works are funded.
entries.literal: Recent income has had convenient paths—the people gain, the state gains, I gain, and merit works are built.

entries.zh: 或以卿之心度我之心，故不能得知。
entries.en: Perhaps you judge me by yourself, and that is why you do not understand.
entries.literal: Perhaps you measure my heart by your heart and therefore cannot know.

entries.zh: 所得財用，暴於天下，不得曲辭辯論。
entries.en: What I receive is open to the world. Do not argue in evasions.
entries.literal: Income obtained is displayed to the realm—no twisting words in debate.

entries.zh: 卿又云女妓越濫，此有司之責，雖然，亦有不同：貴者多畜妓樂，至於勳附若兩掖，亦復不聞家有二八，多畜女妓者。
entries.en: You also complain that courtesans are too many. That is the censors' business, though the cases differ. The great mostly keep musicians, but even meritorious lords and the two palace wings—one seldom hears of a household keeping "two-eight" girls or hoarding courtesans.
entries.literal: You also say female entertainers overflow—this is the responsible officials' duty; still there are differences: the noble mostly keep music girls, but even merit lords and the two flanks—one does not hear of households with "two-eight," or of many keeping female entertainers.

entries.zh: 此並宜具言其人，當令有司振其霜豪。
entries.en: Name every offender. Let the responsible offices strip away their arrogance.
entries.literal: These should all be named; let the offices shake off their frost and pride.

entries.zh: 卿又云：「乃追恨所取爲少，如復傅翼，增其搏噬，一何悖哉。」
entries.en: You also wrote: "They regret having taken too little, and if given wings again they tear all the harder—how perverse!"
entries.literal: You also say: "Yet they regret what they took was little; if given wings again, increasing their tearing and devouring—how perverse!"

entries.zh: 勇怯不同，貪廉各用，勇者可使進取，怯者可使守城，貪者可使捍禦，廉者可使牧民。
entries.en: Courage and cowardice are not the same, nor are greed and integrity. Use the brave for advance, the timid for defense, the greedy for the border, the honest for civil rule.
entries.literal: Bravery and timidity differ; greed and integrity each have their use—the brave may be sent to attack, the timid to hold cities, the greedy to defend the frontier, the upright to rule the people.

entries.zh: 向使叔齊守于西河，豈能濟事？
entries.en: If Shu Qi alone had held the western river, would anything have been accomplished?
entries.literal: Had Shu Qi alone guarded the western river, could the affair have succeeded?

entries.zh: 吳起育民，必無成功。
entries.en: If Wu Qi had only nurtured the people, he would never have succeeded.
entries.literal: Wu Qi nurturing the people would surely have had no success.

entries.zh: 若使吳起而不重用，則西河之功廢。
entries.en: Had Wu Qi not been used as he deserved, the western river would never have been won.
entries.literal: If Wu Qi had not been heavily employed, the achievement at the western river would have been wasted.

entries.zh: 今之文武，亦復如此。
entries.en: The same is true of civil and military men today.
entries.literal: Today's civil and military officers are likewise.

entries.zh: 取其搏噬之用，不能得不重更任，彼亦非爲朝廷爲之傅翼。
entries.en: Use their predatory talents and you cannot avoid employing them heavily again. The court did not give them wings so they could prey harder.
entries.literal: Take their tearing and devouring use—they cannot but be heavily employed again; the court did not give them wings for that purpose.

entries.zh: 卿以朝廷爲悖，乃自甘之，當思致悖所以。
entries.en: You call the court perverse yet still serve it willingly. Ask yourself what makes it perverse.
entries.literal: You call the court perverse yet willingly serve it—you should consider what makes perversity.

entries.zh: 卿云「宜導之以節儉」。
entries.en: You say, "They should be guided by frugality."
entries.literal: You say, "One should guide them with thrift."

entries.zh: 又云「至治者必以淳素爲先」。
entries.en: And, "Perfect government begins in plain simplicity."
entries.literal: And, "Supreme rule must take plain simplicity first."

entries.zh: 此言大善。
entries.en: That is well said.
entries.literal: These words are very fine.

entries.zh: 夫子言「其身正，不令而行；
entries.en: Confucius said, "When the ruler's person is upright, things are done though he does not command;
entries.literal: The Master said, "If his person is upright, without being ordered it is done;

entries.zh: 其身不正，雖令不從」。
entries.en: when his person is not upright, they will not obey though he commands."
entries.literal: if his person is not upright, though ordered they do not follow."

entries.zh: 朕絕房室三十餘年，無有淫佚。
entries.en: I have kept no harem for more than thirty years and have known no debauchery.
entries.literal: I have cut off the inner chambers for thirty-odd years—no licentiousness.

entries.zh: 朕頗自計，不與女人同屋而寢，亦三十餘年。
entries.en: By my own reckoning I have not slept in the same room with a woman for more than thirty years.
entries.literal: I count myself: not sleeping in the same room with women—also thirty-odd years.

entries.zh: 至於居處不過一床之地，雕飾之物不入于宮，此亦人所共知。
entries.en: My living space is no larger than a bed. Ornament does not enter the palace. Everyone knows this.
entries.literal: My dwelling is no more than one bed's space; carved ornament never enters the palace—this too all know.

entries.zh: 受生不飲酒，受生不好音聲，所以朝中曲宴，未嘗奏樂，此羣賢之所觀見。
entries.en: I have never drunk and never cared for music, so at court gatherings no instruments are played. The ministers have seen it themselves.
entries.literal: Since birth I do not drink; since birth I dislike sound—so at court informal feasts music is never played; the worthies have seen this.

entries.zh: 朕三更出理事，隨事多少，事少或中前得竟，或事多至日昃方得就食。
entries.en: I rise in the deep night to work. When business is light I may finish before noon. When it is heavy I eat only after the sun has slanted west.
entries.literal: I rise at the third watch to handle affairs; as affairs vary—few affairs and I may finish before noon; many affairs and only at sundown may I eat.

entries.zh: 日常一食，若晝若夜，無有定時。
entries.en: As a rule I eat once, by day or night, at no set time.
entries.literal: Usually one meal, day or night, at no fixed hour.

entries.zh: 疾苦之日，或亦再食。
entries.en: When I am ill I may eat twice.
entries.literal: On days of illness, sometimes two meals.

entries.zh: 昔要腹過於十圍，今之瘦削裁二尺餘，舊帶猶存，非爲妄說。
entries.en: Once my belly measured more than ten spans around. Now I am scarcely two feet about the waist. The old belt is still here. I do not lie.
entries.literal: Once my waist was more than ten girths; now I am wasted to barely two feet odd—the old belt still kept; this is no empty claim.

entries.zh: 爲誰爲之？
entries.en: For whom did I do this?
entries.literal: For whom was it done?

entries.zh: 救物故也。
entries.en: For the sake of the living—that is why.
entries.literal: To save the creatures—that is why.

entries.zh: 《書》曰：「股肱惟人，良臣惟聖。」
entries.en: The Documents say, "Arms and legs are the man; worthy ministers make the sage."
entries.literal: The Documents say, "Limbs and arms are the man; good ministers make the sage."

entries.zh: 向使朕有股肱，故可得中主。
entries.en: Had I such ministers, I might have been a passable ruler.
entries.literal: Had I such limbs and arms, I could have been a middling lord.

entries.zh: 今乃不免居九品之下，「不令而行」，徒虛言耳。
entries.en: As it is I remain no better than the lowest grade of ruler. "Without being ordered it is done" is only an empty phrase.
entries.literal: Now I still cannot rise above the ninth grade—"without being ordered it is done" is only empty words.

entries.zh: 卿今慊言，便罔知所答。
entries.en: You press your case so hard that I scarcely know how to reply.
entries.literal: You now speak fully—at once I do not know what to answer.

entries.zh: 卿云「若不及于時大息其民，事至方圖，知無及也」。
entries.en: You wrote, "Fail now to give the people real rest, and plan only when crisis comes—you will know you are already too late."
entries.literal: You say, "If one does not at this time greatly rest the people, and only plans when the affair has arrived, one knows it will be too late."

entries.zh: 如卿此言，卽時便是大役其民，是何處所？
entries.en: By your own logic you are overworking the people right now—where?
entries.literal: By your words, at this very moment you are greatly overworking the people—where is that?

entries.zh: 卿云「國弊民疲」，誠如卿言，終須出其事，不得空作漫語。
entries.en: You say "the realm is hollow and the people exhausted." If that is so, name the facts. Do not speak in empty generalities.
entries.literal: You say "the state is spent and the people weary"—if it is truly as you say, in the end you must state the affairs; you cannot make empty, roaming words.

entries.zh: 夫能言之，必能行之。
entries.en: Who can talk must also act.
entries.literal: One who can speak of it must be able to carry it out.

entries.zh: 富國強兵之術，急民省役之宜，號令遠近之法，並宜具列。
entries.en: Ways to enrich the state and strengthen the army, plans to spare the people and cut corvée, orders for near and far—list them all.
entries.literal: Methods to enrich the state and strengthen the army, measures urgent for resting the people and reducing corvée, commands for the near and far—all should be listed in full.

entries.zh: 若不具列，則是欺罔朝廷，空示頰舌。
entries.en: Fail to list them and you deceive the throne with nothing but lip service.
entries.literal: If you do not list them in full, then you are deceiving the court and showing only cheek and tongue.

entries.zh: 凡人有爲，先須內省，惟無瑕者，可以戮人。
entries.en: Before you judge others, judge yourself. Only the spotless may sit in judgment.
entries.literal: Whenever a man would act, he must first look inward; only one without flaw may punish others.

entries.zh: 卿不得曆詆內外，而不極言其事。
entries.en: You may not slander everyone within and without the palace and still refuse to speak plainly.
entries.literal: You may not go through the court inside and out with slander and not speak to the utmost of the affairs.

entries.zh: 佇聞重奏，當復省覽，付之尚書，班下海內，庶亂羊永除，害馬長息，惟新之美，復見今日。
entries.en: I await your next memorial. I shall read it again, send it to the Masters of Writing, and publish it throughout the realm—so the bad sheep are driven off, the harmful horse stilled, and renewal shines once more.
entries.literal: I await hearing your further memorial; I shall again examine it, entrust it to the Masters of Writing, and promulgate it within the four seas—so that bad sheep may be forever removed, harmful horses long stilled, and the beauty of renewal appear again today.

entries.zh: 久之，遷太府卿。
entries.en: In time he was made Minister of the Grand Treasury.
entries.literal: After a long while he was transferred to Minister of the Grand Treasury.

entries.zh: 太清二年，遷雲騎將軍、中軍宣城王長史。
entries.en: In the second year of Taiqing he became General of the Cloud Cavalry and chief clerk to the Prince of Xuancheng, commander of the central army.
entries.literal: In the second year of Taiqing he was transferred to General of the Cloud Cavalry and Chief Clerk to the Prince of Xuancheng, Commander of the Central Army.

entries.zh: 侯景舉兵襲京師，王移入臺內，留琛與司馬楊曒守東府。
entries.en: When Hou Jing marched on the capital the prince withdrew into the inner palace and left Chen and Marshal Yang Xun to defend the Eastern Palace.
entries.literal: Hou Jing raised troops and struck the capital; the prince moved into the inner palace, leaving Chen and the marshal Yang Xun to hold the Eastern Palace.

entries.zh: 賊尋攻陷城，放兵殺害，琛被槍未至死，賊求得之，轝至闕下，求見僕射王克、領軍朱异，勸開城納賊。
entries.en: The rebels soon broke the city and unleashed slaughter. Chen was speared but lived. They found him, bore him in a litter to the palace gate, and demanded Wang Ke, Vice Director, and Zhu Yi, Commander of the Army, begging them to open the gates to the rebels.
entries.literal: The rebels soon stormed the city, let their soldiers slaughter, and Chen was speared but not killed; the rebels found him, carried him in a litter to the palace gate, and sought audience with Vice Director Wang Ke and Commander of the Army Zhu Yi, urging them to open the city and admit the rebels.

entries.zh: 克等讓之，涕泣而止，賊復轝送莊嚴寺療治之。
entries.en: Wang Ke and the others reproached him until he wept and fell silent. The rebels carried him back to Zhuangyan Monastery to heal his wounds.
entries.literal: Ke and the others rebuked him; weeping, he stopped, and the rebels again carried him in a litter to Zhuangyan Monastery for treatment.

entries.zh: 明年，臺城不守，琛逃歸鄉里。
entries.en: The next year the inner city fell. Chen fled to his home district.
entries.literal: The next year the inner city could not be held; Chen fled home to his native place.

entries.zh: 其年冬，賊進寇會稽，復執琛送出都，以爲金紫光祿大夫。
entries.en: That winter, when the rebels marched on Kuaiji, they seized Chen again and sent him to the capital as Household Counsellor with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
entries.literal: That winter the rebels advanced against Kuaiji, seized Chen again, and sent him back to the capital, making him Household Counsellor with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.

entries.zh: 後遇疾卒，年六十九。
entries.en: He later fell ill and died at sixty-nine.
entries.literal: Later he fell ill and died, aged sixty-nine.

entries.zh: 卿又云「百司莫不奏事，詭競求進」。
entries.en: You also say, "Every office memorializes, scheming for promotion."
entries.literal: You also say, "The hundred offices all memorialize, deviously competing for advancement."

entries.zh: 此又是誰？
entries.en: Who are they? Name them.
entries.literal: Who are these again?

entries.zh: 何者復是詭事？
entries.en: Which are these deceptive affairs again?
entries.literal: Which affairs again are the deceptive matters?

entries.zh: 今不使外人呈事，於義可否？
entries.en: If outsiders may no longer present memorials, is that right in principle?
entries.literal: Now not to let outsiders present affairs—in principle is that permissible?

entries.zh: 無人廢職，職可廢乎？
entries.en: No men, no offices—can you abolish the offices themselves?
entries.literal: Without men offices are abandoned—can offices be abandoned?

entries.zh: 職廢則人亂，人亂則國安乎？
entries.en: Abolish offices and men fall into disorder; men in disorder—and the realm is secure?
entries.literal: Offices abandoned, then men are confused; men confused, then is the state at peace?

entries.zh: 以咽廢飧，此之謂也。
entries.en: Reject the meal because the throat hurts—that is the case.
entries.literal: To reject food because of the throat—this is what is meant.

entries.zh: 若斷呈事，誰屍其任？
entries.en: Cut off memorials—who then answers for the charge?
entries.literal: If presenting affairs is cut off, who bears the responsibility?

entries.zh: 專委之人，云何可得？
entries.en: Where will you find men fit to be trusted with everything alone?
entries.literal: Men exclusively entrusted—how can they be obtained?

entries.zh: 是故古人云：「專聽生姦，獨任成亂。」
entries.en: The ancients said it plainly: "Listen to one voice and treachery is born; trust one man alone and chaos follows."
entries.literal: Therefore the ancients said: "Exclusive listening breeds treachery; sole trust breeds chaos."

entries.zh: 猶二世之委趙高，元後之付王莽。
entries.en: Think of Er Shi handing everything to Zhao Gao, or Empress Yuan giving the realm to Wang Mang.
entries.literal: Just as Er Shi entrusted Zhao Gao, and Empress Yuan entrusted Wang Mang.

entries.zh: 呼鹿爲馬，卒有閻樂望夷之禍，王莽亦終移漢鼎。
entries.en: Call a deer a horse, and in the end Yan Le brings ruin at Wangyi; Wang Mang too shifts the Han throne from its base.
entries.literal: Calling a deer a horse—in the end came the disaster of Yan Le at Wangyi; Wang Mang also finally moved the tripod of Han.

entries.zh: 卿云「吹毛求疵」，復是何人所吹之疵？
entries.en: You wrote "splitting hairs for flaws"—whose flaws? Name him.
entries.literal: You say "splitting hairs for flaws"—again, whose flaws are being split?

entries.zh: 「擘肌分理」，復是何人乎？
entries.en: "Splitting muscle to distinguish principle"—who is that?
entries.literal: "Splitting muscle to distinguish principle"—again, who is it?

entries.zh: 事及「深刻」「繩逐」，並復是誰？
entries.en: When you speak of "severity" and "driving by the cord," who are they?
entries.literal: Matters touching "severity" and "driving by the cord"—again, who are they?

entries.zh: 又云「治、署、邸、肆」，何者宜除？
entries.en: You also named "bureaus, offices, lodges, markets"—which should be abolished?
entries.literal: You also say "administration, offices, lodges, markets"—which ought to be abolished?

entries.zh: 何者宜省？
entries.en: Which should be cut?
entries.literal: Which ought to be reduced?

entries.zh: 「國容戎備」，何者宜省？
entries.en: "State ceremony and armaments"—what should be trimmed?
entries.literal: "State display and military preparedness"—which ought to be reduced?

entries.zh: 何者未須？
entries.en: What is not needed now?
entries.literal: Which are not yet needed?

entries.zh: 「四方屯傳」，何者無益？
entries.en: "Garrisons and relays in all four quarters"—which do no good?
entries.literal: "Relay posts in all four quarters"—which are useless?

entries.zh: 何者妨民？
entries.en: Which harm the people?
entries.literal: Which harm the people?

entries.zh: 何處興造而是役民？
entries.en: Where do you build at the cost of forced labor?
entries.literal: Where is construction that conscripts the people?

entries.zh: 何處費財而是非急？
entries.en: Where is treasure spent on what is not urgent?
entries.literal: Where is wealth spent on what is not urgent?

entries.zh: 若爲「討召」？
entries.en: What of "summons and recruitment"?
entries.literal: As for "summons and recruitment"?

entries.zh: 若爲「征賦」？
entries.en: What of "levies and requisitions"?
entries.literal: As for "levies and requisitions"?

entries.zh: 朝廷從來無有此事，靜息之方復何者？
entries.en: The court has never done such things. What is your plan to bring them to rest?
entries.literal: The court has never had such matters from the beginning—what methods quiet and rest them?

entries.zh: 宜各出其事，具以奏聞。
entries.en: Let each charge be named and reported in full.
entries.literal: Each should state the affair and memorialize it in full.

entries.zh: 琛奉敕，但謝過而已，不敢復有指斥。
entries.en: Chen took the edict and could only apologize. He did not dare remonstrate again.
entries.literal: Chen received the edict and only apologized, not daring to criticize again.

entries.zh: 陳吏部尚書姚察云：夏侯勝有言曰：「士患不明經術；
entries.en: Yao Cha, Chen Director of the Ministry of Personnel, said: Xiahou Sheng once said, "The scholar's trouble is not knowing the classics;
entries.literal: Yao Cha, Chen Director of the Ministry of Personnel, said: Xia Hou Sheng had a saying: "The gentleman's trouble is not knowing the classics;

entries.zh: 經術明，取青紫如拾地芥耳。」
entries.en: Once the classics are clear, rank and office are like picking up a mustard plant from the ground."
entries.literal: once the classics are clear, taking blue and purple is like picking up a mustard plant from the ground."

entries.zh: 朱异、賀琛並起微賤，以經術逢時，致於貴顯，符其言矣。
entries.en: Zhu Yi and He Chen both rose from humble beginnings; the classics brought them to high rank in their day—exactly as he said.
entries.literal: Zhu Yi and He Chen both rose from humble beginnings; by the classics they met their time and reached noble eminence—this matched his words.

entries.zh: 而异遂徼寵倖，任事居權，不能以道佐君，苟取容媚。
entries.en: Yet Yi sought favor and power, held office, and could not guide his lord by the Way—only by pleasing and flattering.
entries.literal: Yet Yi went on to seek favor and fortune, hold office and wield power, and could not assist his lord by the Way but only sought to please and flatter.

entries.zh: 及延寇敗國，實异之由。
entries.en: When the rebel ravaged the realm, the blame was truly Yi's.
entries.literal: When the rebel prolonged his ravaging of the state, the fault was truly Yi's.

entries.zh: 禍難旣彰，不明其罪，至於身死，寵贈猶殊。
entries.en: Once disaster was plain his guilt went unnamed; even in death his honors were lavish.
entries.literal: Once disaster was plain, his guilt was not made clear; even at his death, favors and gifts were still extraordinary.

entries.zh: 罰旣弗加，賞亦斯濫，失於勸沮，何以爲國？
entries.en: No punishment fell, rewards ran wild—how can a state encourage good and restrain evil like this?
entries.literal: Punishment was not applied, reward likewise ran wild—failure in encouragement and restraint; how can such a thing be called a state?

entries.zh: 君子是以知太清之亂，能無及是乎。
entries.en: A gentleman therefore knows that the chaos of Taiqing could not have stopped short of this.
entries.literal: The gentleman therefore knows that the chaos of Taiqing could not fail to reach this.

entries.zh: 梁書卷第三十八 列傳第三十二
entries.en: Book of Liang, Volume 38, Biography 32
entries.literal: Book of Liang, Volume 38, Biography 32

entries.zh: 元法僧，魏氏之支屬也。
entries.en: Yuan Faseng belonged to a cadet line of Northern Wei.
entries.literal: Yuan Faseng was a collateral branch of the Wei house.

entries.zh: 其始祖道武帝。
entries.en: His line traced back to Emperor Daowu.
entries.literal: His founding ancestor was Emperor Daowu.

entries.zh: 父鐘葵，江陽王。
entries.en: His father Zhongkui held the title Prince of Jiangyang.
entries.literal: His father was Zhongkui, Prince of Jiangyang.

entries.zh: 法僧仕魏，歷光祿大夫，後爲使持節、都督徐州諸軍事、徐州刺史，鎮彭城。
entries.en: In Wei service he reached Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, then held full staff authority as area commander of Xuzhou forces, inspector of Xuzhou, with his seat at Pengcheng.
entries.literal: Faseng served Wei, rose through Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, and later became Bearer of the Staff with Full Powers, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs in Xuzhou, Inspector of Xuzhou, and garrisoned Pengcheng.

entries.zh: 普通五年，魏室大亂，法僧遂據鎮稱帝，誅鋤異己，立諸子爲王，部署將帥，欲議匡復。
entries.en: When Putong year 5 brought chaos to Wei, Faseng took his post, crowned himself, purged rivals, made his sons kings, and arrayed commanders for a campaign to restore the throne.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Putong the Wei house fell into great disorder; Faseng seized his garrison, declared himself emperor, executed and uprooted dissenters, enfeoffed his sons as kings, deployed generals and commanders, and intended to discuss restoring the dynasty.

entries.zh: 旣而魏亂稍定，將討法僧。
entries.en: As Wei’s turmoil subsided, the court turned to punish Faseng.
entries.literal: Before long the Wei disorder eased somewhat, and they were about to attack Faseng.

entries.zh: 法僧懼，乃遣使歸款，請爲附庸，高祖許焉，授侍中、司空，封始安郡公，邑五千戶。
entries.en: Terrified, Faseng sent envoys to swear allegiance and ask for protected status. Emperor Wu agreed, made him Palace Attendant and Minister of Works, and created him Duke of Shian with five thousand households.
entries.literal: Faseng was afraid and sent envoys to submit in good faith, asking to become a vassal; Emperor Wu assented, appointing him Palace Attendant and Minister of Works, enfeoffing him as Duke of Shian commandery with a fief of five thousand households.

entries.zh: 及魏軍旣逼，法僧請還朝，高祖遣中書舍人朱异迎之。
entries.en: As Wei troops closed in, Faseng begged to come south; the emperor sent Zhu Yi of the Secretariat to receive him.
entries.literal: When Wei armies had already pressed close, Faseng asked to return to court; Emperor Wu dispatched Zhu Yi, Gentleman Attendant of the Secretariat for Drafting, to welcome him.

entries.zh: 旣至，甚加優寵。
entries.en: On arrival he was showered with honors.
entries.literal: Once he arrived, he was greatly favored and indulged.

entries.zh: 時方事招攜，撫悅降附，賜法僧甲第女樂及金帛，前後不可勝數。
entries.en: The court was wooing turncoats, and Faseng received mansions, musicians, gold, and silk beyond counting.
entries.literal: At the time they were actively recruiting and reassuring defectors; he was granted mansions, female musicians, gold and silk—countless gifts before and after.

entries.zh: 法僧以在魏之日，久處疆埸之任，每因寇掠，殺戮甚多，求兵自衛，詔給甲仗百人，出入禁闥。
entries.en: Years on the border in Wei service had left him with many enemies from raiding; he asked for a guard, and the throne gave him a hundred armored men and access to the inner palace.
entries.literal: Because during his Wei days Faseng had long held frontier duties and in every raid had killed many, he requested troops for self-protection; an edict granted him a hundred sets of armor and weapons, with leave to enter and leave the inner palace gates.

entries.zh: 大通二年，加冠軍將軍。
entries.en: In Datong year 2 he was made General of the Champion.
entries.literal: In the second year of Datong he was promoted to General of the Champion.

entries.zh: 中大通元年，轉車騎將軍。
entries.en: Zhongdatong year 1 brought promotion to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
entries.literal: In the first year of Zhongdatong he was transferred to General of Chariots and Cavalry.

entries.zh: 四年，進太尉，領金紫光祿。
entries.en: In the fourth year he advanced to Grand Commandant and concurrently held the title Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with the Golden Ornament.
entries.literal: In the fourth year he advanced to Grand Commandant and concurrently held Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with the Golden Ornament.

entries.zh: 其年，立爲東魏主，不行，仍授使持節、散騎常侍、驃騎大將軍、開府同三司之儀、郢州刺史。
entries.en: The same year he was named sovereign of Eastern Wei—a title he never exercised—yet kept staff authority, Regular Attendant, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, Three-Duke ceremonial rank with an open office, and the Yingzhou inspectorate.
entries.literal: That year he was installed as ruler of Eastern Wei but did not take it up; still he received Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, privileges equal to the Three Dukes with an open office, and the post of Inspector of Yingzhou.

entries.zh: 大同二年，徵爲侍中、太尉，領軍師將軍，薨，時年八十三。
entries.en: Datong year 2 recalled him as Palace Attendant and Grand Commandant with the Army Instructor generalship; he died at eighty-three.
entries.literal: In the second year of Datong he was summoned as Palace Attendant and Grand Commandant, concurrently Army Instructor General; he died at the age of eighty-three.

entries.zh: 二子景隆、景仲，普通中隨法僧入朝。
entries.en: His sons Jinglong and Jingzhong followed him to Liang during Putong.
entries.literal: He had two sons, Jinglong and Jingzhong, who in Putong accompanied Faseng to court.

entries.zh: 神念少善騎射，旣老不衰，嘗於高祖前手執二刀楯，左右交度，馳馬往來，冠絕羣伍。
entries.en: A superb horse-archer even in old age, he once rode before Emperor Wu wielding twin sabers and shields, weaving them left and right at full gallop until none in the host could match him.
entries.literal: Shenian had been skilled in mounted archery from youth; even in old age he did not decline, and once before Emperor Wu he grasped two sabers and shields in his hands, crossing them left and right as he charged back and forth on horseback, surpassing the whole company.

entries.zh: 時復有楊華者，能作驚軍騎，並一時妙捷，高祖深歎賞之。
entries.en: Yang Hua, who could startle an army with his horsemanship, shared the spotlight; the emperor delighted in both men.
entries.literal: At the time there was also Yang Hua, who could perform startling cavalry maneuvers; both were marvels of agility for their age, and Emperor Wu deeply admired them.

entries.zh: 中大通四年，詔爲使持節、都督瑕丘諸軍事、安北將軍、兗州刺史，隨太尉元法僧北討。
entries.en: Zhongdatong year 4 made him full staff bearer, Xiqiu area commander, General Who Pacifies the North, and Yanzhou inspector on Yuan Faseng’s northern campaign.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Zhongdatong he was appointed Full Staff Bearer, Area Commander of Xiqiu forces, General Who Pacifies the North, and Inspector of Yanzhou, to join the Grand Commandant Yuan Faseng on the northern campaign.

entries.zh: 法僧先啓云：「與侃有舊，願得同行。」
entries.en: Faseng had already written, “Kan and I are old friends—I ask to campaign at his side.”
entries.literal: Faseng had first memorialized: “I have old ties with Kan and wish to march together.”

entries.zh: 高祖乃召侃問方略，侃具陳進取之計。
entries.en: The emperor called Kan in for strategy, and Kan set out a complete plan of attack.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor then summoned Kan to ask strategy; Kan laid out a full plan of conquest.

entries.zh: 高祖因曰：「知卿願與太尉同行。」
entries.en: The emperor said, “I know you want to march with the Grand Commandant.”
entries.literal: The High Ancestor then said: “I know you wish to go with the Grand Commandant.”

entries.zh: 侃曰：「臣拔跡還朝，常思效命，然實未曾願與法僧同行。
entries.en: Kan answered, “Since I came south I have lived to serve—but I never wanted to travel with Faseng.
entries.literal: Kan said: “Your servant, having torn himself from the north to return to court, constantly thinks of giving his life, yet in truth I never wished to go with Faseng.

entries.zh: 北人雖謂臣爲吳，南人已呼臣爲虜，今與法僧同行，還是羣類相逐，非止有乖素心，亦使匈奴輕漢。」
entries.en: The north calls me a southerner; the south calls me a turncoat. Marching with Faseng would still look like birds of a feather—and teach the barbarians to scorn the Han.”
entries.literal: Northerners already call me a Wu man; southerners already call me a barbarian captive—if I now go with Faseng, I am still one flock chasing another, which not only betrays my heart but also makes the Xiongnu despise Han.”

entries.zh: 高祖曰：「朝廷今者要須卿行。」
entries.en: The emperor said, “The court needs you on this march.”
entries.literal: The High Ancestor said: “The court now must have you go.”

entries.zh: 乃詔以爲大軍司馬。
entries.en: He was named Grand Army Marshal by edict.
entries.literal: An edict then appointed him Grand Army Marshal.

entries.zh: 高祖謂侃曰；
entries.en: The emperor told Kan:
entries.literal: The High Ancestor said to Kan:

entries.zh: 「軍司馬廢來已久，此段爲卿置之。」
entries.en: “Army Marshal has been empty for years—I restore it for you.”
entries.literal: “The post of Army Marshal has long been vacant; this time it is set up for you.”

entries.zh: 行次官竹，元樹又於譙城喪師。
entries.en: At Guanzhu, Yuan Shu lost his force at Qiao.
entries.literal: On the march, at Guanzhu, Yuan Shu again lost his army at Qiao.

entries.zh: 軍罷，入爲侍中。
entries.en: The expedition over, he returned as Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When the campaign ended, he entered court as Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 五年，封高昌縣侯，邑千戶。
entries.en: Year 5 made him Marquis of Gaochang, fief of one thousand households.
entries.literal: In the fifth year he was enfeoffed Marquis of Gaochang with a fief of a thousand households.

entries.zh: 六年，出爲雲麾將軍、晉安太守。
entries.en: Year 6 sent him out as General of the Cloud Banner and Jin’an grand administrator.
entries.literal: In the sixth year he went out as General of the Cloud Banner and Grand Administrator of Jin’an.

entries.zh: 閩越俗好反亂，前後太守莫能止息，侃至討擊，斬其渠帥陳稱、吳滿等，於是郡內肅清，莫敢犯者。
entries.en: Min-Yue custom bred revolt; no prior governor had quelled it. Kan struck, killed the chiefs Chen Cheng and Wu Man, and the district went still—none dared raise a hand.
entries.literal: The Min and Yue peoples were prone to rebellion; no former administrator had been able to stop it. When Kan arrived he attacked, beheaded the ringleaders Chen Cheng and Wu Man, and thereafter the commandery was quiet and none dared offend.

entries.zh: 頃之，徵太子左衛率。
entries.en: Soon he was recalled as Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard.
entries.literal: Before long he was summoned as Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard.

entries.zh: 大同三年，車駕幸樂游苑，侃預宴。
entries.en: Datong year 3 brought the emperor to Leyou Gardens; Kan joined the feast.
entries.literal: In the third year of Datong the imperial carriage visited the Leyou Gardens; Kan was among those feasted.

entries.zh: 時少府奏新造兩刃槊成，長二丈四尺，圍一尺三寸，高祖因賜侃馬，令試之。
entries.en: The palace workshops had finished a new double-edged spear—twenty-four feet long, thirteen inches around—and the emperor gave Kan a horse to test it.
entries.literal: The Palace Storehouse then reported that a new double-edged spear was complete, twenty-four feet long and thirteen inches in girth; the High Ancestor therefore gave Kan a horse and bade him try it.

entries.zh: 侃執槊上馬，左右擊刺，特盡其妙，高祖善之，又制《武宴詩》三十韻以示侃，侃卽席應詔，高祖覽曰：「吾聞仁者有勇，今見勇者有仁，可謂鄒、魯遺風，英賢不絕。」
entries.en: Kan mounted, spear in hand, and fenced with flawless grace. Delighted, the emperor wrote thirty rhymes of “Martial Feast Poetry” and Kan answered at once from his seat. The emperor read them and said, “They say the benevolent are brave—today I see brave men who are benevolent. Zou and Lu live on; worthies never die out.”
entries.literal: Kan took the spear, mounted, and thrust left and right with consummate skill; the High Ancestor was pleased and also composed thirty rhymes of “Martial Feast Poetry” to show Kan, who answered on the spot at imperial command. The High Ancestor read it and said: “I have heard that the benevolent are brave; now I see that the brave are benevolent—one may say the legacy of Zou and Lu, worthy men unbroken.”

entries.zh: 六年，遷司徒左長史。
entries.en: Year 6 moved him to Left Chief Clerk under the Minister of Education.
entries.literal: In the sixth year he was transferred to Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education.

entries.zh: 八年，遷都官尚書。
entries.en: Year 8 made him Minister of Justice.
entries.literal: In the eighth year he was transferred to Minister of Justice.

entries.zh: 時尚書令何敬容用事，與之並省，未嘗遊造。
entries.en: He Jingrong of the Secretariat held sway; Kan shared his ministry but never visited him.
entries.literal: At the time the Director of the Imperial Secretariat He Jingrong held power; Kan shared the ministry with him but never paid social calls.

entries.zh: 有宦者張僧胤候侃，侃曰：「我床非閹人所坐。」
entries.en: The eunuch Zhang Sengyin came to call; Kan said, “My bed is not for eunuchs.”
entries.literal: A eunuch, Zhang Sengyin, came to wait on Kan; Kan said: “My couch is not for castrated men to sit on.”

entries.zh: 竟不前之，時論美其貞正。
entries.en: He would not receive him—and men praised his integrity.
entries.literal: In the end, Kan would not receive him; contemporaries praised his uprightness.

entries.zh: 九年，出爲使持節、壯武將軍、衡州刺史。
entries.en: Year 9 sent him out with full staff, General of Majestic Martiality, and the Hengzhou inspectorate.
entries.literal: In the ninth year he went out as Full Staff Bearer, General of Majestic Martiality, and Inspector of Hengzhou.

entries.zh: 二年，復爲都官尚書。
entries.en: Year 2 restored him as Minister of Justice.
entries.literal: In the second year he was again Minister of Justice.

entries.zh: 侯景反，攻陷歷陽，高祖問侃討景之策。
entries.en: Hou Jing rebelled and seized Liyang; the emperor asked Kan how to crush him.
entries.literal: Hou Jing rebelled and took Liyang; the High Ancestor asked Kan for a plan against Jing.

entries.zh: 侃曰：「景反跡久見，或容豕突，宜急據採石，令邵陵王襲取壽春。
entries.en: Kan said, “Jing’s treachery has been obvious for years. He may still rush like a cornered boar—seize Caishi at once and let the Prince of Shaoling take Shouchun.
entries.literal: Kan said: “Jing’s treason has long been plain; he may yet charge like a boar, but we should swiftly hold Caishi and have the Prince of Shaoling seize Shouchun.

entries.zh: 景進不得前，退失巢窟，烏合之衆，自然瓦解。」
entries.en: Block his advance, cut off his refuge, and this mob will scatter on its own.”
entries.literal: If Jing cannot advance and loses his nest, this rabble will break up of itself.”

entries.zh: 議者謂景未敢便逼京師，遂寢其策，令侃率千餘騎頓望國門。
entries.en: Councillors said Jing would not dare march on the capital yet; the plan died, and Kan was told to hold a thousand horse before the Wang Gate.
entries.literal: The debaters said Jing would not dare press the capital at once; the plan was shelved, and Kan was ordered to lead a thousand-odd horsemen to encamp before the Wang Gate.

entries.zh: 景至新林，追侃入副宣城王都督城內諸軍事。
entries.en: When Jing reached Xinlin, Kan was recalled into the city to serve as deputy to the Prince of Xuancheng, who commanded all military affairs within the walls.
entries.literal: When Jing reached Xinlin, Kan was recalled into the city to serve as deputy to the Prince of Xuancheng, who commanded all military affairs within the walls.

entries.zh: 時景旣卒至，百姓競入，公私混亂，無復次第。
entries.en: Jing struck too fast; people poured through the gates in chaos, public and private alike.
entries.literal: Jing had come so suddenly that commoners rushed in together; public and private were chaos, order gone.

entries.zh: 侃乃區分防擬，皆以宗室間之。
entries.en: Kan divided the walls into sectors and posted imperial clansmen along each line.
entries.literal: Kan then divided sectors for defense, interposing kinsmen of the imperial house throughout.

entries.zh: 軍人爭入武庫，自取器甲，所司不能禁，侃命斬數人，方得止。
entries.en: Soldiers stormed the armory for arms; officials could not stop them until Kan had several beheaded.
entries.literal: Soldiers fought to enter the armory and take weapons for themselves; the officials could not stop them until Kan ordered several men beheaded—then it ceased.

entries.zh: 及賊逼城，衆皆恟懼，侃偽稱得射書，云「邵陵王、西昌侯已至近路」。
entries.en: As the enemy closed in, panic spread; Kan claimed a captured dispatch: “The Prince of Shaoling and the Marquis of Xichang are almost here.”
entries.literal: When the bandits pressed the wall the host panicked; Kan falsely announced he had intercepted a letter saying “the Prince of Shaoling and the Marquis of Xichang have already reached the near road.”

entries.zh: 衆乃少安。
entries.en: The city steadied a little.
entries.literal: The host was somewhat calmed.

entries.zh: 賊攻東掖門，縱火甚盛，侃親自距抗，以水沃火，火滅，引弓射殺數人，賊乃退。
entries.en: The rebels hit the eastern side gate with fire; Kan met them himself, drowned the flames, shot down several men, and drove them back.
entries.literal: The bandits attacked the eastern side gate, setting a great fire; Kan personally resisted, dousing the flames with water; when the fire died he drew his bow and shot several men dead, and the bandits withdrew.

entries.zh: 加侍中、軍師將軍。
entries.en: He was made Palace Attendant and General of the Army Instructor.
entries.literal: He was promoted Palace Attendant and General of the Army Instructor.

entries.zh: 有詔送金五千兩，銀萬兩，絹萬匹，以賜戰士，侃辭不受。
entries.en: The throne sent five thousand taels of gold, ten thousand of silver, and ten thousand bolts of silk for the troops; Kan refused it.
entries.literal: An edict sent five thousand taels of gold, ten thousand taels of silver, and ten thousand bolts of silk to reward the warriors; Kan declined to accept.

entries.zh: 部曲千餘人，並私加賞賚。
entries.en: His own following of a thousand men he rewarded from his purse.
entries.literal: To his personal following of more than a thousand he gave private rewards besides.

entries.zh: 賊爲尖頂木驢攻城，矢石所不能制，侃作雉尾炬，施鐵鏃，以油灌之，擲驢上焚之，俄盡。
entries.en: The rebels raised pointed wooden “donkeys” proof against shot and stone; Kan devised pheasant-tail torches tipped with iron, oil-soaked, and burned the engines to ash.
entries.literal: The bandits built pointed wooden donkeys to assault the wall, which arrows and stones could not stop; Kan made pheasant-tail torches with iron heads, soaked them in oil, and hurled them onto the donkeys to burn them—all were soon consumed.

entries.zh: 賊又東西兩面起土山，以臨城，城中震駭，侃命爲地道，潛引其土，山不能立。
entries.en: They piled earthworks east and west to dominate the walls; terror rose until Kan tunneled under them and stole their fill—the mounds collapsed.
entries.literal: The bandits also raised earthen hills east and west to overlook the wall; the city was shaken with fear until Kan ordered tunnels dug to draw off the earth so the hills could not stand.

entries.zh: 賊又作登城樓車，高十餘丈，欲臨射城內，侃曰：「車高緌虛，彼來必倒，可臥而觀之，不勞設備。」
entries.en: They built assault towers ten rods high to rain arrows into the city. Kan said, “Too tall, ropes too slack—they will topple. Lie back and watch; no need to prepare.”
entries.literal: The bandits also built tower-carts for assault, more than ten rods high, intending to shoot down into the city; Kan said: “The cart is high and the ropes slack—when it comes it must fall; we may watch lying down without troubling to prepare.”

entries.zh: 及車動果倒，衆皆服焉。
entries.en: The tower moved and fell; the whole city believed him.
entries.literal: When the cart moved it indeed fell; all were convinced.

entries.zh: 賊旣頻攻不捷，乃築長圍。
entries.en: Failing again and again, the rebels threw up a long siege line.
entries.literal: The bandits, having attacked repeatedly without success, then built a long encirclement.

entries.zh: 朱异、張綰議欲出擊之，高祖以問侃，侃曰：「不可。
entries.en: Zhu Yi and Zhang Wan urged a sortie; the emperor asked Kan, who said, “No.
entries.literal: Zhu Yi and Zhang Wan debated sallying out; the High Ancestor asked Kan, and Kan said: “No.

entries.zh: 賊多日攻城，旣不能下，故立長圍，欲引城中降者耳。
entries.en: They could not breach the walls, so they ring us to breed defectors.
entries.literal: The bandits have attacked the city many days and could not take it, so they raise a long encirclement to lure those in the city who would surrender.

entries.zh: 今擊之，出人若少，不足破賊，若多，則一旦失利，自相騰踐，門隘橋小，必大致挫衄，此乃示弱，非騁王威也。」
entries.en: Sortie with few and we achieve nothing; with many, one slip and we will crush each other at the narrow gates and bridges—a rout that shows weakness, not imperial might.”
entries.literal: If we strike now and send few men, we cannot break the bandits; if we send many, one defeat and we will trample one another—the gates are narrow, the bridges small, and we will suffer great rout; this shows weakness, not the spreading of royal majesty.”

entries.zh: 不從，遂使千餘人出戰，未及交鋒，望風退走，果以爭橋赴水，死者太半。
entries.en: They ignored him and sent out a thousand men; before steel met they ran, fought for the bridge, and more than half drowned.
entries.literal: They did not listen and sent a thousand-odd men out; before blades met they fled at sight of the enemy, and in the scramble for the bridge many fell into the water—more than half died.

entries.zh: 初，侃長子躭爲景所獲，執來城下示侃，侃謂曰：「我傾宗報主，猶恨不足，豈復計此一子，幸汝早能殺之。」
entries.en: Jing had taken Kan’s eldest son Dan and brought him under the wall. Kan called, “I have spent my house for the throne and still call it little—why spare one son? Kill him quickly, I beg you.”
entries.literal: Earlier Kan’s eldest son Dan had been taken by Jing and brought beneath the wall to show Kan; Kan said: “I have poured out my clan for the lord and still regret it is not enough—how could I reckon on this one son? I hope you will kill him soon.”

entries.zh: 數日復持來，侃謂躭曰：「久以汝爲死，猶復在邪？
entries.en: Days later they brought him again. Kan said, “I thought you long dead—still here?
entries.literal: Several days later they brought him again; Kan said to Dan: “Long I thought you dead—are you still alive?

entries.zh: 吾以身許國，誓死行陣，終不以爾而生進退。」
entries.en: My body belongs to the realm; I die in the line. You will never move me.”
entries.literal: I have given my body to the state and sworn to die in the ranks; I will never let you govern whether I advance or retreat.”

entries.zh: 因引弓射之。
entries.en: He drew his bow and shot.
entries.literal: Thereupon he drew his bow and shot at him.

entries.zh: 賊感其忠義，亦不之害也。
entries.en: Even the rebels honored his faith and spared the boy.
entries.literal: The bandits were moved by his loyalty and did not harm the son either.

entries.zh: 景遣儀同傅士哲呼侃與語曰：「侯王遠來問訊天子，何爲閉距，不時進納？
entries.en: Jing sent Fu Shizhe, Compeer of the Third Rank, to parley: “The marquis has come far to greet the Son of Heaven—why shut the gates?
entries.literal: Jing sent the Compeer of the Third Rank Fu Shizhe to call Kan and speak: “The marquis has come from afar to inquire after the Son of Heaven—why do you shut him out and not admit him in good time?

entries.zh: 尚書國家大臣，宜啓朝廷。」
entries.en: You are a pillar of the realm—you should speak to the throne.”
entries.literal: The Director is a great minister of the state and ought to report to the court.”

entries.zh: 侃曰：「侯將軍奔亡之後，歸命國家，重鎮方城，懸相任寄，何所患苦？
entries.en: Kan said, “After your flight you were trusted with a great frontier command—what grievance could you have?
entries.literal: Kan said: “After the marquis fled and submitted to the state, he was entrusted with a great frontier post—what hardship could he suffer?

entries.zh: 忽致稱兵？
entries.en: Why draw swords now?
entries.literal: Why suddenly raise arms?

entries.zh: 今驅烏合之卒，至王城之下，虜馬飲淮，矢集帝室，豈有人臣而至於此？
entries.en: You herd this mob to the capital—barbarian horses at the Huai, arrows at the throne. What subject ever did this?
entries.literal: Now you drive this rabble to the royal city; barbarian horses drink at the Huai, arrows cluster at the imperial hall—has any subject ever come to this?

entries.zh: 吾荷國重恩，當稟承廟算，以掃大逆耳，不能妄受浮說，開門揖盜。
entries.en: I owe the dynasty a great debt; I execute the court’s design and scourge traitors—I will not heed sweet lies and open the gate to thieves.
entries.literal: Your servant bears heavy grace from the state and must carry out the temple’s plan to sweep away great treason—I cannot rashly accept empty words and open the gate to welcome robbers.

entries.zh: 幸謝侯王，早自爲所。」
entries.en: Marquis, see to your own end.”
entries.literal: I beg the marquis to look to his own end soon.”

entries.zh: 士哲又曰：「侯王事君盡節，不爲朝廷所知，正欲面啓至尊，以除姦佞，旣居戎旅，故帶甲來朝，何謂作逆？」
entries.en: Shizhe said, “The marquis served with perfect loyalty and the court misunderstood him. He only wished to see the emperor and purge villains—being in the field he wore armor. How is that treason?”
entries.literal: Shizhe also said: “The marquis served his lord with utmost loyalty yet was not understood by the court; he only wished to face the Supreme One and remove wicked ministers—being in the army he therefore came in armor; how is that rebellion?”

entries.zh: 侃曰：「聖上臨四海將五十年，聰明叡哲，無幽不照，有何姦佞而得在朝？
entries.en: Kan said, “Our sage has ruled fifty years, clear-sighted to the deepest shadow—what villains still sit in court?
entries.literal: Kan said: “The sage lord has held the four seas nearly fifty years, bright and wise, nothing hidden in the darkest place—what wicked ministers could remain at court?

entries.zh: 欲飾其非，寧無詭說。
entries.en: To dress up crime, of course there are clever lies.
entries.literal: To gloss over wrong, surely there are crafty words.

entries.zh: 且侯王親舉白刃，以向城闕，事君盡節，正若是邪！」
entries.en: And you yourself brought naked steel to the palace—is that loyalty?”
entries.literal: Moreover the marquis himself raised bare blades against the gate-towers—serving one’s lord with utmost loyalty, is it truly thus?”

entries.zh: 士哲無以應，乃曰：「在北之日，久挹風猷，每恨平生，未獲披敘，願去戎服，得一相見。」
entries.en: Shizhe was silent, then said, “In the north I long admired you and regretted we never met. Let me doff armor and see you once.”
entries.literal: Shizhe had no reply and then said: “In the north I long admired your wind and virtue and always regretted in this life I never met you face to face; I wish to lay aside armor and see you once.”

entries.zh: 侃爲之免胄，士哲瞻望久之而去。
entries.en: Kan took off his helmet; Shizhe stared a long time and left.
entries.literal: Kan removed his helmet for him; Shizhe gazed a long while and departed.

entries.zh: 其爲北人所欽慕如此。
entries.en: Northerners revered him to that degree.
entries.literal: Such was the esteem in which northerners held him.

entries.zh: 羊鴉仁，字孝穆，太山鉅平人也。
entries.en: Yang Yaren, styled Xiaomu, came from Juping in Taishan.
entries.literal: Yang Yaren, styled Xiaomu, was a man of Juping in Taishan commandery.

entries.zh: 少驍果有膽力，仕郡爲主簿。
entries.en: Young he was bold and strong and served the commandery as recorder.
entries.literal: In youth he was fierce and daring, with courage and strength; he served the commandery as chief clerk.

entries.zh: 普通中，率兄弟自魏歸國，封廣晉縣侯。
entries.en: In Putong he brought his brothers south from Wei and was made Marquis of Guangjin.
entries.literal: In the Putong era he led his brothers back from Wei to the homeland and was enfeoffed Marquis of Guangjin county.

entries.zh: 征伐青、齊間，累有功績，稍遷員外散騎常侍、歷陽太守。
entries.en: Fighting in Qing and Qi he won honors, rising to Extraordinary Attendant and Liyang grand administrator.
entries.literal: In campaigns between Qing and Qi he accumulated merit and was gradually promoted to Extraordinary Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Administrator of Liyang.

entries.zh: 中大通四年，爲持節、都督譙州諸軍事、信威將軍、譙州刺史。
entries.en: Zhongdatong year 4 made him staff bearer, Qiao area commander, General of Trustworthy Awe, and Qiaozhou inspector.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Zhongdatong he was made Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander of all military affairs for Qiao province, General of Trustworthy Awe, and Inspector of Qiaozhou.

entries.zh: 大同七年，除太子左衛率，出爲持節、都督南、北司、豫、楚四州諸軍事、輕車將軍、北司州刺史。
entries.en: Datong year 7 brought Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, then staff bearer over southern and northern Si, Yu, and Chu, General of Light Chariots, and Northern Sizhou inspector.
entries.literal: In the seventh year of Datong he was appointed Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, then went out as Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander of all military affairs for the Southern and Northern Si, Yu, and Chu provinces, General of Light Chariots, and Inspector of Northern Sizhou.

entries.zh: 侯景降，詔鴉仁督士州刺史桓和之、仁州刺史湛海珍等精兵三萬，趨懸瓠應接景，仍爲都督豫司淮冀殷應西豫等七州諸軍事、司豫二州刺史，鎮懸瓠。
entries.en: When Hou Jing submitted, Yaren was told to lead Huan Hezhi of Shizhou, Zhan Haizhen of Renzhou, and thirty thousand picked men to Xuanhu to meet Jing—and to command seven provinces from Yu to Western Yu as Si-Yu inspector, based at Xuanhu.
entries.literal: When Hou Jing surrendered, an edict ordered Yaren to supervise Huan Hezhi, Inspector of Shizhou, Zhan Haizhen, Inspector of Renzhou, and others with thirty thousand elite troops to hurry to Xuanhu to link with Jing; he also served as Area Commander of all military affairs for the seven provinces of Yu, Si, Huai, Ji, Yin, Ying, and Western Yu, and as Inspector of Si and Yu provinces, stationed at Xuanhu.

entries.zh: 會侯景敗於渦陽，魏軍漸逼，鴉仁恐糧運不繼，遂還北司，上表陳謝。
entries.en: Jing lost at Woyang and Wei closed in; Yaren, afraid grain would not follow, pulled back to Northern Si and apologized by memorial.
entries.literal: Jing was defeated at Woyang and Wei forces pressed closer; fearing his supply line would fail, Yaren returned to Northern Si and submitted a memorial apologizing.

entries.zh: 高祖大怒，責之，鴉仁懼，又頓軍於淮上。
entries.en: The High Ancestor raged and blamed him; Yaren, afraid, camped again on the Huai.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor was furious and rebuked him; Yaren in fear halted his army on the Huai.

entries.zh: 及侯景反，鴉仁率所部入援。
entries.en: When Jing turned rebel, Yaren marched his command to the rescue.
entries.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled, Yaren led his troops to the capital in relief.

entries.zh: 太清二年，景旣背盟，鴉仁乃與趙伯超及南康王會理共攻賊於東府城，反爲賊所敗。
entries.en: Taiqing year 2: Jing broke faith; Yaren, Zhao Bochao, and Prince Huili of Nankang struck the rebels at the Eastern Directorate and were beaten in turn.
entries.literal: In the second year of Taiqing, after Jing broke the alliance, Yaren joined Zhao Bochao and Prince Huili of Nankang to attack the rebels at the Eastern Directorate compound but was in turn defeated by the rebels.

entries.zh: 臺城陷，鴉仁見景，爲景所留，以爲五兵尚書。
entries.en: The inner city fell; Yaren presented himself to Jing, who held him and named him Minister of the Five Weapons.
entries.literal: When the capital fortress fell, Yaren went to see Jing and was detained by him, appointed Minister of the Five Weapons.

entries.zh: 鴉仁常思奮發，謂所親曰：「吾以凡流，受寵朝廷，竟無報效，以答重恩。
entries.en: Yaren brooded on a reckoning and told his intimates, “I am nobody, yet the throne raised me—and I have never repaid that debt.
entries.literal: Yaren often thought of striking back and told those close to him: “I am but common clay, yet the court favored me, and I have utterly failed to repay that deep grace.

entries.zh: 社稷傾危，身不能死，偷生苟免，以至於今。
entries.en: The realm crumbled and I would not die; I stole life and slipped away, and so it has gone.
entries.literal: The altars tottered and I could not die—I clung to life and escaped, until today.

entries.zh: 若以此終，沒有餘憤。」
entries.en: If I end like this, I shall die with resentment still unspent.”
entries.literal: To end this way leaves every grievance unspent.”

entries.zh: 因遂泣下，見者傷焉。
entries.en: He wept as he spoke; all who heard were stricken.
entries.literal: and he wept; those who saw it were grieved.

entries.zh: 三年，出奔江西，其故部曲數百人迎之，將赴江陵，至東莞，爲故北徐州刺史荀伯道諸子所害。
entries.en: Year 3 he fled into Jiangxi; a few hundred veterans met him bound for Jiangling—but at Dongguan the sons of ex–Northern Xuzhou inspector Xun Bodao killed him.
entries.literal: In the third year he fled west to Jiangxi; several hundred of his old followers welcomed him; he was bound for Jiangling but at Dongguan was murdered by the sons of the former Inspector of Northern Xuzhou, Xun Bodao.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：高祖革命受終，光期寶運，威德所漸，莫不懷來，其皆殉難投身，前後相屬。
entries.en: The historian writes: The High Ancestor took the throne and lit the age with fortune; his power drew every heart, and men threw themselves into death for the realm in endless succession.
entries.literal: The historian writes: The High Ancestor received the mandate in revolution and shone with the fortune of the age; where his power and virtue reached, none failed to come in heart—and they died for the state one after another.

entries.zh: 元法僧之徒入國，並降恩遇，位重任隆，擊鐘鼎食，美矣。
entries.en: Yuan Faseng and his kind who came south were heaped with favor—heavy office, high rank, bells and tripods at feast: glorious.
entries.literal: Yuan Faseng and men like him who entered the realm were all showered with grace, given weighty posts and lofty rank, bell and tripod at table—splendid indeed.

entries.zh: 而羊侃、鴉仁值太清之難，並竭忠奉國。
entries.en: Yet Kan and Yaren met the Taiqing disaster and gave the state their utmost loyalty.
entries.literal: Yet Yang Kan and Yaren met the calamity of Taiqing and both poured out loyalty for the state.

entries.zh: 侃則臨危不撓，鴉仁守義殞命，可謂志等松筠，心均鐵石，古之殉節，斯其謂乎！
entries.en: Kan never bent under danger; Yaren kept faith and died—wills like pine and bamboo, hearts like iron and stone: the martyrs of old, was it not for such as these?
entries.literal: Kan unbent in peril; Yaren kept faith and gave his life—they may be said to match pine and bamboo in will, iron and stone in heart; of the martyrs of old, is this not meant?

entries.zh: 景仲封枝江縣公，邑千戶，拜侍中、右衛將軍。
entries.en: Jingzhong received Zhijiang duke with a thousand households and posts as Palace Attendant and General of the Right Guard.
entries.literal: Jingzhong was enfeoffed Duke of Zhijiang county with a fief of one thousand households and appointed Palace Attendant and General of the Right Guard.

entries.zh: 大通三年，增封，並前爲二千戶，仍賜女樂一部。
entries.en: Datong year 3 enlarged his fief to two thousand households and gave him a company of palace musicians.
entries.literal: In the third year of Datong his enfeoffment was increased, bringing the total to two thousand households, and he was also granted a troupe of female musicians.

entries.zh: 出爲持節、都督廣、越等十三州諸軍事、宣惠將軍、平越中郎將、廣州刺史。
entries.en: He then took staff authority over Guang and Yue as General Who Proclaims Grace, Pacifier of Yue, and Guangzhou inspector.
entries.literal: He was sent out as Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs in Guang, Yue, and the other provinces, General Who Proclaims Grace, Inspector General Who Pacifies Yue, and Inspector of Guangzhou.

entries.zh: 大同中，徵侍中、左衛將軍。
entries.en: During Datong he was recalled as Palace Attendant and General of the Left Guard.
entries.literal: In Datong he was summoned as Palace Attendant and General of the Left Guard.

entries.zh: 兄景隆後爲廣州刺史。
entries.en: His elder brother Jinglong later became Inspector of Guangzhou.
entries.literal: His elder brother Jinglong later became Inspector of Guangzhou.

entries.zh: 侯景作亂，以景仲元氏之族，遣信誘之，許奉爲主。
entries.en: When Hou Jing rebelled, he sent word to entice Jingzhong, a member of the Yuan imperial clan, promising to install him as ruler.
entries.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled, because Jingzhong was of the Yuan clan, Jing sent envoys to entice him, promising to set him up as sovereign.

entries.zh: 景仲乃舉兵，將下應景。
entries.en: Jingzhong mobilized to link arms with Hou Jing from the south.
entries.literal: Jingzhong thereupon raised troops, intending to march down and join Jing.

entries.zh: 會西江督護陳霸先與成州刺史王懷明等起兵攻之，霸先徇其衆曰：「朝廷以元景仲與賊連從，謀危社稷，今使曲江公勃爲刺史，鎮撫此州。」
entries.en: Chen Baxian of the West River commandery and Chengzhou inspector Wang Huaiming rose against him. Baxian told the soldiers, “The throne judges Yuan Jingzhong in league with Hou Jing and a danger to the realm. Duke Bo of Qujiang is coming as your new inspector.”
entries.literal: Just then Chen Baxian, Supervisor of the West River, and Wang Huaiming, Inspector of Chengzhou, among others, raised forces to attack him; Baxian proclaimed to the troops: “The court holds that Yuan Jingzhong has marched with the bandits and plots against the altars of state; it now sends Bo, Duke of Qujiang, as inspector to pacify this province.”

entries.zh: 衆聞之，皆棄甲而散，景仲乃自縊而死。
entries.en: At the news his army melted away; Jingzhong strangled himself.
entries.literal: When the crowd heard this, all cast off armor and scattered; Jingzhong then hanged himself.

entries.zh: 子貞，大同中，求隨魏使崔長謙至鄴葬父，還拜太子舍人。
entries.en: His son Zhen, in Datong, traveled north with envoy Cui Changqian to bury his father at Ye, came back, and became Attendant of the Heir Apparent.
entries.literal: His son Zhen, in Datong, asked to follow the Wei envoy Cui Changqian to Ye to bury his father, then returned and was appointed Attendant of the Heir Apparent.

entries.zh: 太清初，侯景降，請元氏戚屬，願奉爲主，詔封貞爲咸陽王，以天子之禮遣還北，會景敗而返。
entries.en: Early Taiqing brought Hou Jing’s offer to crown a Yuan prince; Zhen was made Prince of Xianyang and sent north in state, but Hou Jing’s fall sent him home again.
entries.literal: At the opening of Taiqing, when Hou Jing surrendered, he asked for a Yuan kinsman to set up as sovereign; an edict enfeoffed Zhen Prince of Xianyang and sent him north with imperial ceremony, but Jing was defeated before he could go and he returned.

entries.zh: 楊華，武都仇池人也。
entries.en: Yang Hua came from Chouchi in Wudu.
entries.literal: Yang Hua was a native of Chouchi in Wudu.

entries.zh: 父大眼，爲魏名將。
entries.en: His father Yang Dayan was one of Wei’s great commanders.
entries.literal: His father Dayan was a famed general of Wei.

entries.zh: 華少有勇力，容貌雄偉，魏胡太后逼通之，華懼及禍，乃率其部曲來降。
entries.en: Young, strong, and striking in looks, he fled Wei after Empress Dowager Hu forced herself on him, bringing his household guard south.
entries.literal: Hua in youth had courage and strength, a heroic bearing; Empress Dowager Hu of Wei forced him into intimacy; Hua, fearing disaster, led his personal troops to surrender.

entries.zh: 胡太后追思之不能已，爲作《楊白華歌辭》，使宮人晝夜連臂蹋足歌之，辭甚悽惋焉。
entries.en: Hu could not forget him and wrote the “Yang Baihua” lyrics, set palace women to sing them ceaselessly, hand in hand, stamping the measure—the song was heartbreakingly sad.
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager could not stop longing for him and composed the song lyrics “Yang Baihua,” ordering palace women day and night to link arms, stamp their feet, and sing it—the words were exceedingly mournful.

entries.zh: 華後累征伐，有戰功，歷官太僕卿，太子左衛率，封益陽縣侯。
entries.en: He fought in many campaigns, became Director of the Imperial Stud and Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, and was made Marquis of Yiyang.
entries.literal: Hua later took part repeatedly in campaigns and won merit, rising through Director of the Imperial Stud and Left Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, and was enfeoffed Marquis of Yiyang county.

entries.zh: 太清中，侯景亂，華欲立志節，妻子爲賊所擒，遂降之，卒於賊。
entries.en: Taiqing’s Hou Jing rebellion found him wanting to stand firm until bandits seized his family; he submitted and died in their camp.
entries.literal: In Taiqing, when Hou Jing rebelled, Hua wished to hold to integrity, but his wife and children were seized by the bandits, so he surrendered and died among them.

entries.zh: 鶤字子鵬。
entries.en: Kun, styled Zipeng.
entries.literal: Kun, courtesy name Zipeng.

entries.zh: 隨侃臺內，城陷，竄於陽平。
entries.en: He followed Kan inside the palace; when the city fell he hid at Yangping.
entries.literal: He followed Kan within the palace compound; when the city fell he hid at Yangping.

entries.zh: 侯景呼還，待之甚厚。
entries.en: Hou Jing called him back and favored him richly.
entries.literal: Hou Jing summoned him back and treated him very generously.

entries.zh: 及景敗，鶤密圖之，乃隨其東走。
entries.en: When Jing fell, Kun plotted in secret and followed him east.
entries.literal: When Jing was defeated, Kun secretly plotted against him and went east with him.

entries.zh: 景于松江戰敗，惟餘三舸，下海欲向蒙山。
entries.en: Jing lost on the Song River with three boats left and put to sea for Mengshan.
entries.literal: Jing was defeated on the Song River and had only three boats left; he went downriver intending to make for Mengshan.

entries.zh: 會景倦晝寢，鶤語海師：「此中何處有蒙山！
entries.en: Jing fell asleep at midday; Kun told the pilot, “There is no Mengshan here—
entries.literal: Jing, weary, napped by day; Kun spoke to the sea pilot: “Where is there any Mengshan in these waters!

entries.zh: 汝但聽我處分。」
entries.en: do as I say.”
entries.literal: You need only obey my orders.”

entries.zh: 遂直向京口。
entries.en: They bore straight for Jingkou.
entries.literal: They then headed straight for Jingkou.

entries.zh: 至胡豆洲，景覺，大驚，問岸上人，云「郭元建猶在廣陵」，景大喜，將依之。
entries.en: At Hudou Isle Jing woke in panic and hailed the bank: “Guo Yuanjian still holds Guangling”—Jing was overjoyed and meant to go to him.
entries.literal: At Hudou Isle, Jing woke, greatly alarmed, and asked people on the shore, who said, “Guo Yuanjian is still at Guangling”; Jing rejoiced and meant to join him.

entries.zh: 鶤拔刀叱海師，使向京口。
entries.en: Kun bared his blade and drove the pilot toward Jingkou.
entries.literal: Kun drew his sword and shouted at the sea pilot to steer for Jingkou.

entries.zh: 景欲透水，鶤抽刀斫之，景乃走入船中，以小刀抉船，鶤以槊入刺殺之。
entries.en: Jing tried to swim clear; Kun hacked at him. Jing fled into the cabin and picked at the planking with a knife—Kun ran him through with a spear.
entries.literal: Jing tried to slip overboard; Kun struck with his blade. Jing ran into the hold and gouged the hull with a small knife; Kun thrust in with a spear and killed him.

entries.zh: 世祖以鶤爲持節、通直散騎常侍、都督青、冀二州諸軍事、明威將軍、青州刺史，封昌國縣公，邑二千戶，賜錢五百萬，米五千石，布絹各一千匹，又領東陽太守。
entries.en: Emperor Yuan gave Kun staff authority, Regular Attendant, Qing-Ji area command, General of Bright Awe, and Qingzhou inspector; made him Duke of Changguo, two thousand households; five million cash, five thousand piculs of grain, a thousand bolts each of cloth and silk; and Grand Administrator of Dongyang besides.
entries.literal: Emperor Yuan made Kun Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary, Area Commander of all military affairs for Qing and Ji provinces, General of Bright Awe, and Inspector of Qingzhou; enfeoffed him Duke of the State of Changguo with a fief of two thousand households; granted five million cash, five thousand piculs of grain, and a thousand bolts each of cloth and silk; and he also held the post of Grand Administrator of Dongyang.

entries.zh: 征陸納，加散騎常侍。
entries.en: Kun campaigned against Lu Na and received the additional title of Regular Attendant.
entries.literal: Kun campaigned against Lu Na and was given the additional title of Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 平峽中，除西晉州刺史。
entries.en: The gorges pacified, he became Western Jinzhou inspector.
entries.literal: When the mid-Yangzi gorges were pacified he was appointed Inspector of Western Jinzhou.

entries.zh: 破郭元建於東關，遷使持節、信武將軍、東晉州刺史。
entries.en: Kun defeated Guo Yuanjian at Dong Pass and was promoted to Full Staff Bearer, General of Trustworthy Valor, and Inspector of Eastern Jinzhou.
entries.literal: After Kun defeated Guo Yuanjian at Dong Pass, he was promoted to Full Staff Bearer, General of Trustworthy Valor, and Inspector of Eastern Jinzhou.

entries.zh: 承聖三年，西魏圍江陵，鶤赴援不及，從王僧愔征蕭勃於嶺表。
entries.en: In 554, Western Wei besieged Jiangling. Kun arrived too late to help and then accompanied Wang Sengyin against Xiao Bo in Lingnan.
entries.literal: In the third year of Chengsheng, Western Wei besieged Jiangling; Kun could not reach them in time and followed Wang Sengyin on the campaign against Xiao Bo in Lingnan.

entries.zh: 聞太尉僧辯敗，乃還，爲侯瑱所破，於豫章遇害，時年二十八。
entries.en: When word came that Grand Marshal Sengbian had fallen, Kun turned back. Hou Tian routed him, and Kun was killed at Yuzhang at the age of twenty-eight.
entries.literal: Hearing that Grand Marshal Sengbian had been defeated, Kun turned back; Hou Tian defeated him, and he was killed at Yuzhang, aged twenty-eight.

entries.zh: 元樹，字君立，亦魏之近屬也。
entries.en: Yuan Shu, styled Junli, was another near kinsman of the Wei imperial house.
entries.literal: Yuan Shu, courtesy name Junli, was likewise a close kinsman of Wei.

entries.zh: 祖獻文帝。
entries.en: His grandfather was Emperor Xianwen.
entries.literal: His grandfather was Emperor Xianwen.

entries.zh: 父僖，咸陽王。
entries.en: His father Xi held the title Prince of Xianyang.
entries.literal: His father Xi was Prince of Xianyang.

entries.zh: 樹仕魏爲宗正卿，屬尒朱榮亂，以天監八年歸國，封爲鄴王，邑二千戶，拜散騎常侍。
entries.en: In Wei he was Director of the Imperial Clan; after Erzhu Rong’s upheaval he defected in Tianjian year 8, was made Prince of Ye with two thousand households, and became Regular Attendant.
entries.literal: Shu served Wei as Director of the Imperial Clan; when Erzhu Rong’s turmoil broke out, he came over in the eighth year of Tianjian, was enfeoffed Prince of Ye with a fief of two thousand households, and appointed Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 普通六年，應接元法僧還朝，遷使持節、督郢司霍三州諸軍事、雲麾將軍、郢州刺史，增封並前爲三千戶。
entries.en: Putong year 6 saw him escort Faseng home, then take staff command over Ying, Si, and Huo as General of Cloudlike Pennants and Yingzhou inspector, with his fief raised to three thousand households.
entries.literal: In the sixth year of Putong he went out to meet Yuan Faseng on his return to court, was transferred to Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs in Ying, Si, and Huo, General of Cloudlike Pennants, and Inspector of Yingzhou, and his enfeoffment was increased to three thousand households in all.

entries.zh: 討南蠻賊，平之，加散騎常侍、安西將軍，又增邑五百戶。
entries.en: A campaign against southern rebels succeeded; he gained Regular Attendant, General Who Pacifies the West, and five hundred more households.
entries.literal: He campaigned against southern barbarian bandits, pacified them, was promoted to Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Pacifies the West, and his fief was again increased by five hundred households.

entries.zh: 中大通二年，徵侍中、鎮右將軍。
entries.en: Zhongdatong year 2 recalled him as Palace Attendant and General Who Guards the Right.
entries.literal: In the second year of Zhongdatong he was summoned as Palace Attendant and General Who Guards the Right.

entries.zh: 四年，爲使持節，鎮北將軍，都督北討諸軍事，加鼓吹一部以伐魏，攻魏譙城，拔之。
entries.en: Year 4 gave him staff authority as General Who Guards the North and commander of the northern expedition, with war drums and orders against Wei; he stormed and seized Qiao.
entries.literal: In the fourth year he became Bearer of the Staff, General Who Guards the North, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Northern Campaign Military Affairs, was granted a suite of war drums, and campaigned against Wei; he attacked the Wei city of Qiao and took it.

entries.zh: 會魏將獨孤如願來援，遂圍樹，城陷被執，發憤卒于魏，時年四十八。
entries.en: Dugu Ruyuan came to relieve the city and then besieged Shu. When the city fell, Shu was captured; he died in Wei of pent-up indignation at forty-eight.
entries.literal: The Wei general Dugu Ruyuan came to the rescue, then besieged Shu; the city fell and he was captured; he died of grief in Wei at the age of forty-eight.

entries.zh: 初，其父每有南歸之志，常謂諸子曰：「人生安可久淹異域，汝等可歸奉東朝。」
entries.en: His father had long wished to return south and often told his sons, “How can a man remain long in a foreign land? You should return and serve the Eastern Court.”
entries.literal: Earlier his father had often wished to return south and would regularly tell his sons: “How can a man long linger in a foreign land? You should go home and serve the Eastern Court.”

entries.zh: 侃至是將舉河濟以成先志。
entries.en: Kan now meant to stir the Yellow and Ji region to honor that vow.
entries.literal: Kan now intended to raise the Yellow and Ji rivers to fulfill that earlier wish.

entries.zh: 兗州刺史羊敦，侃從兄也，密知之，據州拒侃。
entries.en: His cousin Yang Dun, Yanzhou inspector, got wind of the plot and barred the province against him.
entries.literal: Yang Dun, Inspector of Yanzhou, was Kan’s paternal cousin; he learned of it in secret and held the province to resist Kan.

entries.zh: 侃乃率精兵三萬襲之，弗剋，仍築十餘城以守之。
entries.en: Kan hit him with thirty thousand elite troops, failed to take him, and ringed the land with a dozen fortified camps.
